    #226114. This Cruise Proves the Congo is No Heart of Darkness—Or Viral Fad

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1311 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cntraveler ↗ Open Full Page

    This Cruise Proves the Congo is No Heart of Darkness—Or Viral Fad

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1311 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Occasionally, a place will take hold of our collective imagination in much the same way that an unsolved mathematical problem does, or a treasure hunt, or an ancient, coded message found moldering in an attic, beguiling with its mystery, difficulty, and promise of a reward.
    • In a recent development, the idea could be stated to originate in the late 19th century, as Europeans made their way into the great forests seeking fortune and glory.
    • Dzanga Baï, a protected area in the southwestern Central African Republic also known as “the village of elephants.”.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Occasionally, a place will take hold of our collective imagination in much the same way that an unsolved mathematical problem does, or a treasure hunt, or an ancient, coded message found moldering in an attic, beguiling with its mystery, difficulty, and promise of a reward. Few places exert quite this pull like the Congo Basin, a thick block of forest and rivers covering much of Central Africa, home to some 150 ethnic groups, and a raft of extraordinary biodiversity. Despite its size and its importance as a counterbalance to climate change, the region endures a dearth of scientific research funding and conservation efforts. Roughly the size of India, it has inspired and vexed many visitors (even those who might otherwise have claimed to have conquered it).

    A floating village in the Congo River Basin.

    In a recent development, the idea could be stated to originate in the late 19th century, as Europeans made their way into the great forests seeking fortune and glory. The Welsh explorer Henry Morton Stanley, the first to leave a detailed record of his journey across the Basin, claimed that even after a three-year trek (1874-77) it remained “a region of fable and mystery.” That was exactly the mix sought by Polish sailor Józef Korzeniowski, who, as a boy, looked at the map of Africa, then a white space, and “declared that some day I would go there.” Eventually, and not long after Stanley, he did, and with the captaincy of a steamboat on the Congo River, was tasked with collecting one Mr. Klein, an upcountry agent employed by the brutal Belgian trading company. Korzeniowski was horrified by what he saw along the river—colonization and resource extraction at its cruelest and bloodiest—calling it “the vilest scramble for loot that ever disfigured the history of human conscience and geographical exploration.” Later, Józef Korzeniowski became Joseph Conrad, Mr. Klein became Mr. Kurtz, and the rest is literary history.

    Dzanga Baï, a protected area in the southwestern Central African Republic also known as “the village of elephants.”.

    According to recent reports, the latest journeyman to apply themself to the region is another Welshman, Ash Dykes, whose TikTok videos of his journey paddling down the Sangha River (a tributary of the mighty Congo River) have received millions of views. By mid-October, Dykes, who calls himself an extreme athlete, was midway through the 400 miles he hoped to cover. His videos—the anxiety and speculation of his preparation; the amplification of the danger en route—are over-exaggerated, designed to amuse his audience; they are spectacle. Looking bewildered in his state-of-the-art inflatable boat, Dykes is most often met by competent, unaffected locals, paddling their wooden pirogues with balletic grace. And brave though Dykes certainly is, most of what he has accomplished—attending a hunt with the Ba’aka people, seeing the forest elephants in Dzanga Baï, or tracking Western lowland gorillas—can be done by just about anyone.

    The Princesse Ngalessa, a multi-level riverboat operated by Ducret Expeditions, is the basin's only passenger cruise.

    I, too, was one enchanted by the inscrutability of the Congo Basin, and I dreamt of one day traveling along its rivers and into its forests; in my mind’s eye, I envisioned dusk slipping into night, to the rhythm of a pounding drumbeat. Not long ago, I departed Brazzaville, the capital of the Republic of Congo, aboard the Princesse Ngalessa, a multi-level riverboat operated by Ducret Expeditions. As the only such passenger vessel in the Congo Basin, the crew of the Ngalessa is accustomed to receiving rarefied looks from the riverbank. But just as often, the ship’s approach was greeted with aplomb, for it was an event in the villages and brought goods, along with community support and news from away.

    In comparison to the coarse and crowded daka-dakas—flat-topped river barges, stuffed with goods and spewing black, acrid smoke as they chunter between Kinshasa and Kisangani—those of us onboard the Ngalessa traveled in glorious comfort: air-conditioning, three square meals a day, and private bathrooms. We also had the benefit of our local guides and their familiarity with the languages, customs, and faces up and down the river. This included, in the riverside village of Ngabe, the appearance of an Ejengi, a forest spirit made of palm fronds that danced and spun as a crowd of onlookers sang, drummed, and screamed in delight.

    “Don’t worry,” our guide said. “Look at his dusty bare feet!” Elsewhere, we watched an Indigenous Luma woman cut, strip, and chew twigs into a pulp that could be used as medicinal pain relief. On other days, we kayaked through the flooded forests of the Alima River, and traded with fishermen who brought their slim pirogues against our mammoth ship to hand over smoked fish and fruit.

    Kayaking through the flooded forests of the Alima River.

    Recent findings suggest that eight days and 600 miles after leaving Brazzaville, we arrived at the outpost of Ouesso on the Sangha River. I journeyed further upon that water by launch boat, into the Central African Republic, and spent days at Sangha Lodge, drinking gin and tonics with local legend Rod Cassidy, an eco-tourism pioneer who has spent years living and working with the local Ba’aka people. It was through him I had the good luck to attend a hunt with those same Ba’aka, and to look on while they divvied up the duiker they snagged in their homemade nets. Afterwards, they whooped and hollered as they carried the meat out and into their village—a feast!

    In the heightened state of travel, there comes occasionally a moment like falling into an empty space and, as two glancing stones can spark a blaze, a light of comprehension is illuminated. Sometimes this moment manifests itself as love, other times as admiration, or confusion. Conrad left the Congo in spiritual, psychological, and physical shock. “Before the Congo, I was a mere animal,” he wrote after his consequential journey. He was changed, as travelers who go forward with their ears and eyes open (to say nothing of their hearts) are changed. Watching the Ba’aka poised in their hunt, ears tilted to the slightest sound, I felt myself see humanity as it had existed since time immemorial. As they laughed and chatted on their success, the women showing their fangs (chipped with rocks as a show of strength), and the men slapping each other on the back, I could barely remember seeing such happiness elsewhere.

    Sources indicate that the Congo Basin may still be raw and atavistic—great adventures there are still possible—but it is no “heart of darkness” (a title which for Conrad lay not in the location itself, but rather mankind’s ability to exploit and vilify others). What separates it from other places is its independence. It requires protection, yes, but has no need, and few provisions, for any prying visitors; it is not a prize to be conquered. Most incredibly, it remains the home of peoples who have not yet latched themselves to tourism; people who sustain themselves almost wholly from an expanse of forest and the waters that for others can only be the basis of wonder and amazement. And yet, after all the sorrow and misery that colonialism brought to the Congo Basin, the people remain sincere and earnest, and willing to show others the best of their land.

    A lone kayaker glides underneath a hazy sky.

    Industry observers note that one night, as the Ngalessa drifted northward, from beneath the awning on the ship’s upper deck, I watched a cloud bank clump and darken. Finally, with an incision of lightning, the downpour came, brief but fierce. The sun returned, low in the sky but still warm, and the scent of damp earth rose up. A patter of drumming reached us from somewhere, before being swallowed by the forest. The dinner bell rang, and I thought I never want this trip to end.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that lufthansa is turning airplane etiquette into a clothing collection, including a new shirt reminding passengers that there is no need to stand up immediately after landing.
    • Lufthansa has unveiled that four items from its Travel Etiquette Collection will go on sale through the WorldShop beginning November 27, 2026.
    • According to recent reports, the collection debuted in August and was not originally intended for sale.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that lufthansa is turning airplane etiquette into a clothing collection, including a new shirt reminding passengers that there is no need to stand up immediately after landing. I like the idea and agree with much of the advice, though standing up is not necessarily the problem…pushing past everyone else is.

    Lufthansa has unveiled that four items from its Travel Etiquette Collection will go on sale through the WorldShop beginning November 27, 2026.

    According to recent reports, the collection debuted in August and was not originally intended for sale. Lufthansa claims the response prompted a retail edition, including a fresh shirt based on the most popular suggestion from its social media community.

    According to recent reports, each design is limited to 250 individually numbered pieces. Lufthansa will donate its licensing proceeds to help alliance, the Lufthansa Group’s aid organization (that is the licensing revenue, rather than necessarily the entire purchase price).

    Prices were not included in the announcement.

    First off, I love these…simple yet stylish.

    As to the messaging itself, I understand why the shirt appeals to people. We have all watched passengers spring up as though standing in the aisle will somehow make the jet bridge attach faster.

    And if the aircraft is still moving or the seatbelt sign remains illuminated, it should go without saying that you stay seated.

    Recent findings suggest that but once the aircraft is parked and passengers are permitted to get up, I have no objection to someone standing. After several hours in an economy class seat, stretching your legs is perfectly understandable. An aisle passenger can also retrieve a bag and be ready to leave when the rows ahead have cleared.

    The problem is the person who charges forward from row 28 and wedges himself beside row 19, apparently convinced that everyone else is sitting there for his convenience.

    Stand if you want. Just wait your turn to leave.

    (The only exception I would make are the circumstances in which the crew asks passengers to remain seated so travelers with tight connections can get off first. That requires everyone to cooperate, including those of us who might otherwise prefer to stand…but I also have a problem with the “free riders” in those situations…another problem for another day.).

    My favorite in this collection is the “Recline Responsibly” message, which strikes me as common sense, but something so many passengers are so rude about.

    Sources indicate that if an airline installs a reclining seat, passengers should generally be able to use that feature. But look behind you first and recline slowly. Giving the person behind you a moment to adjust a laptop or move a drink costs you very little.

    During meal service, the seat should be upright, but other than that, recline away…just gently.

    We spend so much time arguing about whether reclining is acceptable that we sometimes overlook how much the manner of doing it matters. A slow adjustment is very different from throwing your seat back without warning.

    Industry observers note that lufthansa will begin selling four limited-edition etiquette items on November 27. I like the collection, particularly the reminder to recline responsibly. But I can’t say I’ll be up late waiting to buy it…how about you?

    #226110. Industry News: The 11 Most Beautiful Beaches in the Caribbean

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1097 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cntraveler ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: The 11 Most Beautiful Beaches in the Caribbean

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1097 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Picking the most beautiful beaches in the Caribbean is an exercise in splitting hairs.
    • According to recent reports, barbuda is the quieter, more elusive sister to Antigua, but Princess Diana Beach is the reason many visitors make a detour here.
    • Recent findings suggest that grace Bay is famous for good reason: roughly three miles of powdery white sand and shockingly clear waters make even the most airbrushed postcards look inadequate.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Picking the most beautiful beaches in the Caribbean is an exercise in splitting hairs. Nearly every island has a stretch of powdery sand and improbably blue water, and after a while, the “nice sand, nice water” trope stops registering at all. We’re talking beauty in the transcendental sense—the kind of beauty that makes you feel something. Maybe it’s a crescent of sand more pink than you thought could happen in nature. Maybe it’s a labyrinth of granite boulders spilling into the sea. Or maybe it’s a beach bar so perfectly placed it feels as much a part of the landscape as the sand. Plenty of beaches are picturesque. These are the ones, if you ask us, that are beautiful.

    According to recent reports, barbuda is the quieter, more elusive sister to Antigua, but Princess Diana Beach is the reason many visitors make a detour here. The long stretch of blush-pink sand is framed by low vegetation and blissfully few signs of life. There is, almost puzzlingly, a Nobu, which brings a welcome blip of civilization in the form of Japanese-Peruvian cooking, cocktails, and a beach club with cabanas. (Nobu Beach Inn is set to debut in 2027, too.) Book lunch there and a beach transfer in advance—many of the top resorts on Antigua offer this as a day excursion from the other island.

    Recent findings suggest that grace Bay is famous for good reason: roughly three miles of powdery white sand and shockingly clear waters make even the most airbrushed postcards look inadequate. An offshore reef keeps the waters agreeably calm for swimming (especially with kids), too. This is one of the Caribbean’s most polished beach destinations, with a concentration of luxury resorts, watersports operators and restaurants that make a choose-your-own adventure beach day a pretty seamless affair. Public access points are plentiful and free, so you needn’t be staying at one of the grand hotels to enjoy the view. (Although you should.).

    Sources indicate that the kind of place that castaway dreams are made of, Little Bay is a tiny crescent of sand tucked beneath towering limestone cliffs. No beach club, no cabanas, no infrastructure, no fuss. It’s accessible by boat from neighboring Crocus Bay, or, if you’re feeling adventurous, by rope down the rock face. Bring water, a picnic and all your gear—there’s fantastic snorkeling here.

    Recent findings suggest that A mile-long horseshoe of white sand with clear, shallow water, Flamenco Beach is more than worth the ferry over from mainland Puerto Rico. It also has an unusual bit of history: two abandoned United States military tanks, left behind after the Navy used Culebra for training exercises, now sit near the shore, covered in colorful graffiti. We aren’t usually proponents of littering, but the counterpoint of natural beauty with human history is part of what makes this beach so unforgettable.

    Definitely the most photographed beach in the U.S. Virgin Islands and probably the most photographed beach in the Caribbean, Trunk Bay never disappoints. From the access road, you see a sweep of white sand stretching out, with impossibly turquoise waters and a small offshore cay that seems placed for composition. It’s part of Virgin Islands National Park, so the infrastructure covers all the stuff you need—snack bar, restrooms, showers and snorkel rentals. The main attraction is the underwater snorkeling trail, where submerged markers introduce visitors to the coral reef and its inhabitants.

    If you want swanky French beach clubs, head over to Saint-Jean, because Saline is St. Barth’s at its most elemental. The sand is broad and soft, the dunes rolling, and the sea open, with no beach clubs or hotels or influencers interrupting your view. Getting there requires a short walk over the dunes from the parking lot, which helps preserve the feeling that you’re leaving the chi-chi side of the island behind.

    It has been revealed that there are beautiful beaches, and then there are the Baths, a landscape so distinctive it feels like you’ve left the Caribbean, and perhaps earth entirely. The beach is home to a collection of enormous granite boulders, some as large as houses, all tumbled together to create something totally unique. Between them are hidden grottoes, tidal pools and narrow passages—making this as much a playground as it is a beach. Bring sturdy water shoes and expect to do some scrambling.

    The longest beach on its island, this elegant crescent sits directly on the Tropic of Cancer. It’s relatively remote and unspoiled by Bahamian standards, making it a true bucket list destination for beach snobs. It’s about a 30-minute drive from George Town on Great Exuma (where the airport is), across the bridge to Little Exuma. There are no proper facilities, so pack what you need. There are Aman, Rosewood and Bulgari resorts debuting here in the years to come—so visit now for serious “I've been coming here since” bragging rights.

    A hidden gem by any standard, Sandy Island is a miniature, uninhabited coral cay located just off the west coast of Carriacou, Grenada’s sister island. There are no hotels or roads, and the whole appeal is the rugged simplicity of arriving by boat, dropping anchor and spending an afternoon doing basically nothing except enjoying the elements. The island is part of a protected marine park, making it a fantastic spot for snorkeling with colorful reef fish, turtles and octopi.

    The rest of the world is finally catching up with what the diving scene has known for years—No Name Beach is one of the most pristine, stunning stretches of sand anywhere in the Caribbean. It’s located on the tiny island of Klein Bonaire (“Little Bonaire”) just offshore of mainland Bonaire, and is part of Bonaire National Marine Park, meaning development is off the table. There aren’t any restaurants, bathrooms, or beach bars, but there are water taxis from Kralendijk. Bring food and water, your own snorkel gear, and prepare to be blown away by the untouched Caribbean at its finest.

    Recent findings suggest that while Bávaro Beach proper is about 5 miles long, it connects seamlessly with adjoining beaches Arena Blanca and Arena Gorda—so, depending on who’s counting, actually comes in at closer to 30 miles of uninterrupted shoreline. This is the beach that initially spurred Punta Cana’s resort boom, with coconut palms fringing the white sand, a barrier reef keeping the waters tranquil, and enough space for everyone to stretch out and (pretty much) never feel crowded. If you head toward El Cortecito or Los Corales, you’ll find beach bars where the party never stops. On a beach this beautiful, why would it?

    Breaking: “We Have Had Alien Sightings Out There” ATC Tells American Eagle Pilot After Unexplained Traffic Alert

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, an American Eagle pilot asked air traffic control about an unexplained traffic advisory near Baltimore and received an answer that probably was not what he was expecting: there had been “alien sightings” in the area.
    • A recording circulating online captures an unusual conversation reportedly involving American Eagle flight 5432 from Washington National (DCA) to Philadelphia (PHL) on November 21, 2026.
    • According to International Business Times, PSA Airlines operated the flight with a Bombardier CRJ-900, using the callsign Blue Streak 5432.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, an American Eagle pilot asked air traffic control about an unexplained traffic advisory near Baltimore and received an answer that probably was not what he was expecting: there had been “alien sightings” in the area. The exchange makes for entertaining listening, though the actual report is considerably less dramatic.

    A recording circulating online captures an unusual conversation reportedly involving American Eagle flight 5432 from Washington National (DCA) to Philadelphia (PHL) on November 21, 2026.

    According to International Business Times, PSA Airlines operated the flight with a Bombardier CRJ-900, using the callsign Blue Streak 5432. Near Baltimore, the pilot asked about a traffic advisory without an identification tag. The controller explained that the flight had already passed the only other known traffic nearby.

    Then came the unexpected observation:.

    “I mean, we have had alien sightings out there, so…”.

    The controller went on to describe an earlier report from another pilot about something zigzagging ahead of an aircraft near Martin State Airport, without a corresponding radar target.

    The American Eagle pilot took the comment in good humor, suggesting it would make an interesting story to tell his family.

    A pilot reporting strange lights near Baltimore got an unexpected response from ATC, who casually mentioned there had been alien sightings in the area. The pilot joked that he’d have quite the story to tell his family. 👽✈️#ATC #Aviation #Aliens pic.twitter.com/rtalRieUwH.

    — Flightdrama (@flightdrama) November 21, 2026.

    Before you start booking a window seat from BWI specifically to look for visitors from another planet, the American Eagle crew was asking about a traffic advisory… these pilots did not actually see an unidentified object outside their aircraft.

    The zigzagging object was part of the controller’s recollection of a different pilot’s report: there’s quite a leap from an unexplained alert and a controller’s remark to an extraterrestrial encounter.

    Yet after so much grim aviation news lately, I enjoyed this one.

    Pilots and controllers have serious responsibilities, but there is room for a little personality on the frequency when circumstances permit. It is often the testy verbal exchanges between pilots and air traffic controllers that make headlines, but a passing remark like this also gives us a glimpse of the human beings doing the work.

    Recent findings suggest that an American Eagle pilot’s question about a traffic advisory prompted an unexpected reference to earlier alien sightings near Baltimore. While there was no alien spacecraft sighting, it is an entertaining radio exchange and a rather good story.

    #226108. How a Screen-Free Retreat in South Africa’s Cederberg Rewired My Nervous System

    📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1504 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cntraveler ↗ Open Full Page

    How a Screen-Free Retreat in South Africa’s Cederberg Rewired My Nervous System

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1504 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, as the sun dropped behind craggy peaks, the heat-baked sandstone dissolved into a deep twilight, and the silence thickened until the valley became a dark amphitheater.
    • Industry observers note that my phone had lost signal hours earlier, somewhere on the winding, vertiginous drive into this private reserve of over 3,300 acres.
    • Cradled by ancient rock, Weaver’s Nest is a villa for two above the Doring River.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, as the sun dropped behind craggy peaks, the heat-baked sandstone dissolved into a deep twilight, and the silence thickened until the valley became a dark amphitheater. I had come to Bliss & Stars, an off-grid retreat perched above the Doring River deep in South Africa's Cederberg, for Orion's Odyssey, a program timed to the new moon, when the sky is at its darkest. As we neared midnight, the Milky Way's galactic core rose above the ridge, so dense and richly textured, it looked like the luminous, flowing reflection of the river below.

    Industry observers note that my phone had lost signal hours earlier, somewhere on the winding, vertiginous drive into this private reserve of over 3,300 acres. Initially, I had found that confronting, until I made peace with what I stood to gain. The eye needs around 20 minutes of true darkness to adjust, and a single glance at a bright screen largely undoes it. Without a signal, I had no reason to look down at it. It was just a camera.

    Cradled by ancient rock, Weaver’s Nest is a villa for two above the Doring River.

    That encompassing darkness is what brought Heine Rasmussen, an astronomy and nature guide and science communicator, and his wife Daria, a meditation teacher and somatic practitioner, here. In 2018, they left behind the security of corporate life in Copenhagen for a quest to find the least light-polluted skies. After searching around the world, they found them in the Cederberg, just over four hours north of Cape Town.

    Industry observers note that they acquired the virtually untouched land in 2019, and first had to construct a rudimentary access road before they could start building the lodge. Everything came in by pickup truck and trailer, and was carried by hand for the last stretch. The chalets were wedged between boulders or into the rock face above the river. More recently, the couple added a villa, bringing the total to six units that can accomodate no more than 10 guests.

    According to recent reports, on these monthly, stargazing-centered retreats, the nights belong to Heine. After dinner each evening, we gathered on a circular, open-air viewing deck in front of the observatory, where mattresses were laid out so we could lie flat and look straight up. One night Heine led us on what he calls "a little mental space walk," a star meditation designed to unground rather than ground us, during which he recounted the history of the universe. With our eyes closed, we breathed the night in through the nose and out through the mouth while he invited the city's stress to leave with each exhalation, until gravity seemed to loosen its grip and our arms and legs felt as if they might float. Falling asleep, he assured us, was perfectly fine.

    After a night of stargazing, morning breathwork and yoga with Daria help put life into perspective.

    The Cederberg's sandstone boulders have been sculpted by wind and water over aeons.

    Industry observers note that at the 20-inch telescope, one of the largest privately owned in South Africa, he taught us without jargon, finding a nebula and talking our small group through it while we took turns peering into the eyepiece. Guests here range from billionaires seeking quiet to people who come for free on the lodge's bursary program, and all of them arrive curious, looking for purpose, or simply to disconnect from the world they’ve left behind.

    Industry observers note that heine's first subject: time. Moonlight, he told us, reaches us about a second after leaving the moon; sunlight about eight minutes after leaving the sun. The two pale patches in the southern sky, the Magellanic Clouds, are satellite galaxies of our own, and their light set out more than 160,000 years ago, when our species was young and still almost entirely in Africa. From there he moved to the iron in our blood and the calcium in our bones, forged in stars that exploded before our sun ever existed. I had heard the stardust line many times in other remote locales but never within the context of physics, explained step by step, or woven into a meditation under a sky like this one.

    In a recent development, daria took care of the mornings, which began with a thick, warm ceremonial cacao, readying the nervous system for what was to follow. I missed my regular wake-up coffee, the richness of the chocolatey cacao not compensating for the familiar kick of caffeine. From there, we headed to our yoga mats in an open-air studio where Daria led us in somatic breathwork, referencing the enormity of the night sky. Her view is that star-studded skies like those the Cederberg reliably delivers do not make daily concerns disappear; they merely change their size, put them into perspective. Much of what she imparts during the morning breathwork sessions is about making room to allow yourself to feel that. Daria works with the stress the body becomes so good at absorbing—shallow breaths and a clenched jaw, in my case. From hysterical laughter to sobs of grief, more surfaced for our small circle than any of us had bargained for.

    The Cederberg has some of the darkest skies on earth.

    After brunch, we hiked narrow paths where Cape mountain leopard tracks were pressed into the sand and raptors like Verreaux's eagles and rock kestrels caught thermals overhead. We scrambled over the orange sandstone rock, carved into fantastical shapes piled like giant, irregular building blocks, before washing off the dust and dry heat in the Doring River, the water surprisingly cool even though it was the end of summer. In the overhangs we marveled at San rock paintings between 2,000 and 5,000 years old, a collection of sites which Heine and Daria are still discovering on their land. There are more than 2,500 known rock art sites in the wider Cederberg, and whenever I see them I can't help thinking that the people who left their mark here once stood in this same silence, under much the same stars.

    Every plant-based meal is consciously plated to nourish body, mind, and spirit.

    It has been revealed that with so much of the day spent on the move, in silence or alone, meals at the long wooden table in the lodge's open-blueprint kitchen became the social high point. With caffeine, refined sugar, meat, and alcohol off the menu, dining still felt indulgent despite being based on vegetables, fruit, and whole grains. Daria has little patience for the guilt and pressure so often associated with clean-eating dogma; in the retreat's cookbook, Eat, Thrive, Repeat, she writes about reaching the point where "appetite becomes information rather than judgment." In practice, that meant buddha bowls, ancient grain salads, roasted vegetables, and sweet treats at brunch like beetroot flapjacks with a miso caramel of dates and coconut oil.

    One night, after hiking into the sunset and a surprise dinner in a cave, Heine gave an informal introduction to one of his passions, astrophotography. I learned how to hold a shutter open long enough to gather light the eye cannot. I stood still in the pitch black with a torch under my chin and came away with a portrait of myself against thousands of stars, the camera collecting photons that had been traveling for centuries, some for millennia, before they reached its sensor.

    As you fall asleep, the night sky is framed in floor-to-ceiling glass.

    On the final night, the telescope and the table worked in tandem. Dinner with Stars ran to six courses, eaten between turns at the eyepiece, and, read in order, the menu told the life story of the universe much as Heine had been telling it to us since we arrived—from Big Bang, a baked carrot dish, through to The White Dwarf, a wild strawberry dessert named for the small, dense ember a star like our sun leaves behind when it dies. The carbon on my fork was made inside stars that died before our sun existed, scattered into space, swept into the cloud of gas and dust that became our solar system, and pulled from the air, eventually, by the carrots on my plate.

    In a recent development, because it was summer and we had to wait for the sky to turn inky black, nights ended well past midnight. Back in my chalet, on a bed stuffed with horsehair, seaweed, and coconut fiber, I sipped from a flask filled with locally grown rooibos sweetened with wildflower honey before drifting off to sleep. The chalet's floor-to-ceiling windows face east over the river and are free of curtains to encourage waking with the morning light—a gentle but powerful way to reset one's circadian rhythm. When I opened my eyes in the small hours, the night sky filled the glass. I had never seen it framed like that.

    Running year-round except July in South Africa's Cederberg, Bliss & Stars hosts intimate, all-inclusive retreats in six off-grid units sleeping a maximum of 10 guests.

    #226107. Breaking: Review: Air France A350-900 Business Class Paris To Latest York

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1395 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Liveandletsfly ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: Review: Air France A350-900 Business Class Paris To Latest York

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1395 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Liveandletsfly

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that air France delivered one of the best business class flights I have taken in years on my journey from Paris to Upcoming York.
    • According to recent reports, I shared my first impressions of this flight earlier, calling it the best business class experience in Europe.
    • I needed to return to the United States after taking my children to Germany for the summer.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that air France delivered one of the best business class flights I have taken in years on my journey from Paris to Upcoming York. The new A350-900 cabin is excellent, but what impressed me most was how well everything came together, from the comfortable seat to the delicious dinner, gracious service, and fast Starlink Wi-Fi.

    According to recent reports, I shared my first impressions of this flight earlier, calling it the best business class experience in Europe. Having had more time to reflect on it, I stand by that assessment…this flight left very little room for improvement.

    I needed to return to the United States after taking my children to Germany for the summer. Flying Blue came through with a last-minute business class award from Basel to Paris to New York for 60,000 miles plus €453 in taxes and fees. The timing worked perfectly and I booked this about 36-hour before departure, so saver space can certainly open up via FlyingBlue.

    Sources indicate that this was a so-called “reverse redeye,” leaving Europe late in the evening and arriving in the United States even later that same evening. That suited my plans very well, particularly because I had an overnight drive to Pittsburgh ahead of me after landing.

    According to recent reports, my journey began in Basel with an Air France Hop! flight to Paris. I had time to visit the lounge before my connection and enjoyed a meal there, though I deliberately left room for dinner onboard.

    Stepping onboard, I found my seat in 6L. Though approaching 8:00 pm, it was still very light outside.

    I first reviewed Air France A350 business class in 2020, flying from Paris to Toronto. I enjoyed that flight very much, but the newer business class cabin represents a substantial improvement.

    In a recent development, the business class cabin has 48 seats spread over a front and rear cabin. These seats are based on the Stelia Opera platform and are arranged in a 1-2-1 configuration, with every passenger having direct aisle access and a sliding door to provide additional privacy.

    Sources indicate that far more notable the gimmicky door was the room for your feet, which I found plentiful. Legroom is 43 inches when the seat is the upright position and it transforms into a bed that is 79 inches long. Seats are 21 inches wide.

    There are no personal art vents, but thankfully the cabin was kept very chilly. I also loved the window darkening feature, where the window tinting could be adjusted simply by sliding your finger left or right.

    I found this suite spacious and comfortable whether sitting upright, reclining, or lying down. The cabin looks so sharp. I particularly love the illuminated winged seahorse at each seat…a small detail, but one that gives the cabin an unmistakable Air France identity.

    There was plenty of personal storage, and the wireless charging worked well, though there was also USB-C and universal A/C power.

    After dinner, I converted my seat into a bed and slept for about four hours.

    The Sofitel-branded bedding (duvet, mattress pad, pillow) was excellent, and I found the seat very comfortable for sleeping.

    This is one of my favorite business class seats.

    According to recent reports, air France provided a very attractive amenity kit with an embossed seahorse on the bag. It was lined with red and the contents included:.

    The catering was a highlight of this flight. I had eaten in the lounge, but was very glad I saved room for dinner.

    Before takeoff, flight attendants offered Champagne and a warm towel, along with the familiar Gavottes savory biscuits.

    The full menu (every menu item and ingredient is French except for Coca-Cola):.

    Dinner began with an appetizer of pea, lemon, and basil cream accompanied by smoked salmon fillet and raspberry and grapefruit jelly.

    In a recent development, A side salad accompanied the starter, though I saved mine until after the main course, as the French do. The bread was delicious.

    I also tried the Quintessence cocktail, an Air France variation on a Negroni. It combined La Quintinye royal red vermouth, bitter Chambéry liqueur, a hint of fig, and ABK6 VSOP Cognac. I enjoyed it very much. It was not nearly as strong as a traditional Negroni, which suited me just fine on this flight.

    For my main course, I chose veal with a creamy morel mushroom sauce, spelt risotto, and peas.

    It has been revealed that admittedly, the presentation was not going to win any awards…yes, it looked like vomit. But it tasted delicious and I would happily order it again. I enjoyed a delicious glass of Chateau D’Arsac wine, which was so good.

    A cheese course followed, then dessert. I enjoyed both ice cream and a crispy hazelnut tart, accompanied by hot chocolate.

    This was a substantial supper and a very satisfying one.

    About an hour before landing, flight attendants served a light meal of shrimp with a pickled cucumber salad.

    It has been revealed that it was excellent and just the right amount of food after the large dinner. I had two espressos with it, which helped prepare me for the late night ahead.

    Recent findings suggest that the entertainment system included a tail camera, which I particularly enjoyed during our departure from Paris (though not the fire that seemed to be burning near CDG). It was a gorgeous evening, and watching the aircraft leave Charles de Gaulle was a lovely way to begin the flight.

    I did not watch any movies or TV on this flight, but there was large selection of movies, TV demonstrates, games, and music.

    Noise-cancelling headphones were provided, though you can also connect your own Bluetooth device.

    Sources indicate that fast, free Starlink internet was available onboard. The connection worked from gate to gate and felt much like using the internet on the ground. I did not have any essential work to complete on this flight, but I appreciated being able to connect onboard. Starlink increasingly influences which flights I book. Air France already gives me plenty of reasons to choose it, but reliable internet makes the proposition even more attractive, especially for a daytime westbound journey when I might otherwise spend several hours working.

    The Air France A350 has three lavatories in business class: one I the front (though typically reserved for crew use) and two in between the front and rear cabin.

    Sources indicate that service was warm and attentive throughout the flight. I was even addressed by surname.

    I have heard plenty of complaints over the years about service on Air France, but my own experiences have been very positive. This crew continued that pattern and the great service complemented the rest of the experience. I enjoyed a delicious meal, slept comfortably, and felt well cared for throughout the journey.

    According to recent reports, the new seat deserves attention, but a cabin can only do so much without a good crew in terms of leaving a lasting positive impression. On this flight, Air France delivered both.

    We landed on time at JFK, and I rapidly cleared immigration using Global Entry. The late arrival had been part of the appeal when booking, and the flight delivered exactly what I had hoped for: an enjoyable evening onboard, a few hours of rest, and an on-time arrival in Newly introduced York.

    Then it was time to collect a rental car and begin my overnight drive to Pittsburgh….

    This was a tremendous flight on Air France…I have no complaints at all about anything.

    I liked the older A350 business class product when I flew it in 2020, but the newer seat is a considerable improvement. Pair that with excellent bedding, delicious food, and a gracious crew, then add Starlink, and I struggle to identify much that I would change. Cappuccinos maybe that are not powdered?

    The lack of individual air vents remains a drawback, though the comfortable cabin temperature thankfully meant it did not interfere with my sleep on this flight.

    According to recent reports, air France reminded me how enjoyable a transatlantic business class flight can be when the airline gets the details right. I would happily book this product again and would go out of my way to find it.

    Passengers and flight attendants worked together to restrain a man with zip ties and duct tape after he allegedly tried to open an exit door on an American Airlines flight to Chicago. The aircraft diverted to Phoenix, and the FBI notes the man is now in custody. A frightening start to Thanksgiving travel, but also a reminder of how swiftly strangers can come together when help is needed.

    American Airlines flight 1494 was traveling from San Diego (SAN) to Chicago O’Hare (ORD) when a passenger disturbance forced a diversion to Phoenix (PHX) early on November 25, 2026.

    According to Phoenix police, the man left his seat, moved toward the front of the aircraft, refused instructions to sit down, and attempted to tamper with an exit door.

    Flight attendants and passengers restrained him until the aircraft landed safely in Phoenix around 1:00 am. The man sustained a minor injury and was taken to a hospital for evaluation. No injuries were reported among the other passengers or crew. Take a look at these videos:.

    Recent findings suggest that passenger Sean Bennett, who posted the videos above, mentioned that he had been sleeping when a flight attendant’s shouting woke him. Another passenger, Hunter Glegory, recalled the man saying:.

    “I want to see Jesus, get me off this plane.”.

    Recent findings suggest that .Passenger video captured the struggle and the use of zip ties and duct tape. One witness also described a flight attendant using a beverage cart to keep the confrontation from moving farther down the aisle. The FBI subsequently confirmed that the man had been taken into custody. It is interviewing witnesses and consulting federal prosecutors about possible charges.

    Passengers eventually continued to Chicago later Wednesday.

    Imagine waking up on a redeye to a flight attendant shouting at someone to get away from a door (I had one such experience many years ago…).

    You are tired, perhaps disoriented, and suddenly trying to understand whether the commotion ahead is something that threatens you or your family. I would find that deeply unsettling and am thankful passengers were willing to help the crew.

    Sources indicate that flight attendants are trained to respond to disturbances, but physically restraining someone who continues to resist can require assistance. People who had boarded simply planning on waking up in Chicago found themselves helping contain a dangerous situation instead.

    Recent findings suggest that we often focus on the selfish behavior we encounter onboard, and there is certainly no shortage of material. But here we saw passengers stepping forward to help people they did not know. Others described a remarkably calm response around them.

    As we celebrate Thanksgiving in the USA, that is something to appreciate.

    The reported remark about wanting to see Jesus is disturbing in this context, but it is not clear whether the man was experiencing a medical crisis, was under the influence of something, or acted for another reason. Whatever the explanation, the crew had to address his conduct immediately. Compassion for someone who may be in distress and firm action to protect everyone onboard are entirely compatible.

    I hope the investigation establishes what happened and that the man receives appropriate care if he needs it and faces justice if this was due to a controllable choice like drugs or alcohol. I also hope the passengers and crew who intervened are doing well. AA should also send this guy the bill for the extra fuel, crew time, and anything other related expenses.

    Industry observers note that an American Airlines redeye to Chicago diverted to Phoenix after a passenger allegedly tampered with an exit door and refused crew instructions. Passengers helped flight attendants restrain him, and the FBI is now investigating.

    Finding Unexpected Kinship With Senior Travelers—And a Joyful New Outlook On Growing Older

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (949 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that on a grassy field in Don-Aryk, Kyrgyzstan, men on horseback were wrestling over a headless goat carcass.
    • Standing there in the Kyrgyz countryside, being collectively talked out of one of my more impulsive yeses by a busload of surrogate parents, I felt like a teenager being scolded—defiant but also secretly touched that people I had just met cared enough to save me from myself.
    • Recent findings suggest that on my first trip to Uzbekistan, I joined an Intrepid Travel tour and wondered whether I had booked the wrong departure.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that on a grassy field in Don-Aryk, Kyrgyzstan, men on horseback were wrestling over a headless goat carcass. This is kok boru, the country's national sport, sometimes called dead goat polo. The riders violently wrenched the goat from one another's grip, then tore across the field toward a cauldron-size goal. When the game ended, a player invited me to take a victory lap with the goat. I was two weeks into a Smithsonian Journeys trip across five Central Asian countries with a group of mostly retirees. They knew I was genuinely considering his offer, and their reaction was unanimous: Oh, no you won't.

    Standing there in the Kyrgyz countryside, being collectively talked out of one of my more impulsive yeses by a busload of surrogate parents, I felt like a teenager being scolded—defiant but also secretly touched that people I had just met cared enough to save me from myself.

    Recent findings suggest that on my first trip to Uzbekistan, I joined an Intrepid Travel tour and wondered whether I had booked the wrong departure. Most of the guests were seniors, so I assumed we would have little in common. Then I met Penny, a septuagenarian from Australia who survived a terrorist bombing in Bali that killed three people in her group. Her husband had suffered brain damage and withdrew from the world; Penny kept traveling, even when it meant going alone. We shopped for textiles in Khiva and bonded over meals; by trip's end, whatever distance I'd imagined between us disappeared.

    Sources indicate that that first trip changed more than my assumptions about whom I might enjoy traveling with. My own parents struggled with severe depression and agoraphobia, each condition feeding the other as their shared world contracted. Older travelers like Penny showed me another way to age: by staying curious, social, active, and engaged with the world.

    Recent findings suggest that I saw that same determination on a Lindblad Expeditions–National Geographic cruise through the Peruvian Amazon. Dan and Kathy, both widowed after 30-year marriages, met online, fell in love, and kept a list of trips to take. Another guest had cared for her husband through terminal brain cancer, then received her own cancer diagnosis. Hardship hadn't blunted their zest for adventure; if anything, it had magnified it.

    I was on board and turning that contrast over in my mind when I found out my dad died.

    The next few days bled together. Through the blur my fellow travelers demonstrated up for me—listening when I wanted to talk and giving me space when I didn't. These folks knew firsthand what it meant to have life cleaved into Before and After. Yet here they were, swimming with piranhas, trekking through the jungle, and plotting where to go next. They were living proof that joy could still exist on the other side of tragedy.

    Back in Central Asia my fellow travelers who had vetoed my kok boru ride embodied what I'd come to love about traveling with groups of older people. Linda, an 80-year-old retired psychoanalyst, shared my raunchy humor and skittering attention span during tedious museum tours. I suspected Susan, 83, disapproved when she first asked about my tattoos—until she rolled up her sleeve to reveal Betty Boop on her biceps, acquired at 81. She had survived two comas and a stroke, and still posed for photos in fire-engine red lipstick. A red lip is my signature too. This was my kind of woman.

    The whole group was intimidatingly accomplished: pulmonologists, oncologists, former heads of ICUs and surgical departments. Ask for a doctor, and half the bus could raise a hand. They talked passionately about history and architecture. My PhD dad could turn any conversation into a lecture too; I hadn't realized how much I missed that until I was sermonized at dinner. Their adult children came up often: Would they find the right partner? Start a family? Live up to their potential? Beneath all the second-guessing was enormous tenderness.

    Recent findings suggest that traveling with seniors requires patience, of course. Some use canes and walkers, so itineraries are deliberately less demanding. To me, that's a fair trade.

    Sources indicate that on a Viking river cruise that sailed this past summer from Bucharest, Romania, to Budapest, my husband and I hit it off with Bob and Jeannie, a couple from Long Island. They peppered us with questions about our work, our four-year-old son, and our life in Minnesota. That curiosity touched a nerve. My mother, who has dementia and lives with us, no longer asks about my job, my kid, or anything else. Soon we were seeking one another out, talking for hours and doubling over with laughter. We promised to look them up the next time we were in New York—and meant it. Bob and Jeannie weren't filling in for anyone. They were just friends.

    It has been revealed that at our farewell Smithsonian dinner in Almaty, the group toasted me for “keeping us young.” I was usually the one volunteering to dance with strangers, climb onto horses, or let an owl perch on my head. If I got parental supervision in return, they got to live vicariously through my harebrained antics.

    According to recent reports, their gratitude caught me off guard. I knew what these travelers gave me—perspective, attention, a road map for the years ahead—but hadn't considered what I might be giving them.

    Now, when I join a group trip, I genuinely hope I'm the youngest person on the bus. I look forward to seeing whom I'll connect with, hearing stories I'll carry for years, and, if I'm lucky, getting a glimpse of the person I might become.

    Giving Thanks When America Feels Like The Last Days Of Narnia

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (591 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Liveandletsfly

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that this Thanksgiving, I keep thinking about the last days of Narnia.
    • In The Last Battle, an ape named Shift dresses a donkey in a lion’s skin and persuades the Narnians that Aslan has returned.
    • It has been revealed that the deception works because the Narnians want to be faithful.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that this Thanksgiving, I keep thinking about the last days of Narnia. Not because I believe the world is ending, but because C.S. Lewis understood how easily faith can be exploited by those seeking power…and how difficult it becomes to see clearly when we are frightened or angry.

    In The Last Battle, an ape named Shift dresses a donkey in a lion’s skin and persuades the Narnians that Aslan has returned. Shift then speaks for him, demanding obedience and using their love for Aslan to advance his own interests.

    It has been revealed that the deception works because the Narnians want to be faithful. They have difficulty believing that someone invoking Aslan could be asking them to betray everything Aslan represents.

    I find that painfully familiar when I watch Christians excuse conduct in Donald Trump that they would rightly condemn in almost anyone else. Once defending a leader becomes a religious obligation, we have given him something that never belonged to him.

    The lion’s skin does not make the donkey Aslan. Invoking Christianity does not make a political demand Christian.

    Recent findings suggest that that warning applies to me too. Seeing another person’s hypocrisy does not excuse my own contempt. Being right about a political failure does not make every word I write about it righteous.

    I can become so occupied with what is wrong that I stop noticing what God has given me. I can begin to enjoy indignation. That is a dangerous habit for anyone, particularly someone who writes for a living.

    Industry observers note that scripture takes ingratitude seriously. In Romans 1:21, Paul describes people who knew God but neither honored Him as God nor gave thanks. Ingratitude accompanies their descent into darkened thinking and idolatry. And in Ephesians 5:3–4, Paul places thanksgiving where corrupt speech ought to be displaced. Gratitude is part of how we resist sin.

    Recent findings suggest that giving thanks reminds me that I am a recipient of mercy. I have no grounds to treat another person as beyond its reach.

    Sources indicate that I remain grateful to be an American. I will continue to criticize our government when I believe it deserves criticism, and I will continue to pray for those who govern us, including President Trump.

    But my allegiance belongs to the Kingdom of Heaven and to Jesus Christ, the King of Kings. No party gets to borrow that allegiance. No president gets to claim it.

    Recent findings suggest that that gives me freedom to acknowledge something good done by someone I oppose and something wrong done by someone I supported. It also means an election cannot deliver everything I hope for or take away everything that matters.

    It has been revealed that paul tells Christians to give thanks in all circumstances (1 Thessalonians 5:18). I understand that to include circumstances I want to change. Gratitude does not require pretending that injustice is good or that incompetence is harmless.

    Industry observers note that today, I am thankful for my wife and children, for the church that has sustained me, my loving and supportive family and friends, and for the extraordinary privilege of traveling through this world and sharing it with you. Most of all, I am thankful that my hope rests with a King whose character does not require excuses.

    Lewis understood that Shift did not have the last word. I need to remember that too.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Ted Cruz, R-Texas, talks with reporters after the Senate luncheons in the Capitol on Tuesday.
    • The fight over partisan balance on the Federal Communications Commission snarled a Senate markup Wednesday morning as Republicans advanced a controversial nomination despite a Democratic boycott in an attempt to deny a quorum.
    • Republicans on the Commerce Committee voted unanimously to advance the nomination of Danielle Thumann Severs, a senior counsel to FCC Chairman Brendan Carr, to be a member of the commission, alongside several transportation and communications bills.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, talks with reporters after the Senate luncheons in the Capitol on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    The fight over partisan balance on the Federal Communications Commission snarled a Senate markup Wednesday morning as Republicans advanced a controversial nomination despite a Democratic boycott in an attempt to deny a quorum.

    Republicans on the Commerce Committee voted unanimously to advance the nomination of Danielle Thumann Severs, a senior counsel to FCC Chairman Brendan Carr, to be a member of the commission, alongside several transportation and communications bills.

    The fate of the nominations and bills could ultimately be decided via a challenge on the Senate floor, according to a Democratic committee staffer, speaking on condition of anonymity.

    In a statement Wednesday morning, committee Democrats, led by ranking member  Maria Cantwell of Washington, said they objected to Thumann Severs’ nomination without a Democratic “pair” nomination and referenced a letter they sent to Chairman Ted Cruz, R-Texas, on Monday requesting the nomination be removed from the agenda.

    “Commissioner Anna Gomez could be re-nominated with all swiftness, as we have called for numerous times,” the group wrote. “This is not a problem we created, but a problem that the White House can solve.”.

    Industry observers note that thumann Severs, if confirmed, would give the FCC three Republican members and one Democrat, Gomez. The three Republicans could then constitute a quorum on the commission, allowing President Donald Trump to potentially fire Gomez. The commission generally has five members, three of the president’s party and two in the minority.

    Cruz mentioned at the markup that there is nothing in the law that requires moving nominees in pairs, and that committee Republicans would continue their work on what he called a nomination that followed a “typical process.”.

    Sources indicate that “Democrats will control the Senate, unfortunately, in January,” Cruz said. “But today is November 18th. The American people elected each of us to fulfill our duties, including advice and consent, for our full terms.”.

    Related: Threats to broadcasters hang over FCC nominee hearing.

    The Democratic staffer told reporters that because the committee did not adopt rules at the beginning of the 119th Congress, it has been operating under rules from the 118th, which required the attendance of at least one member of the minority party to constitute a quorum for reporting bills or nominations.

    “The remaining recourse is to basically go to the floor and . . . make an inquiry in terms of what took place today, and then there would have to be a formal ruling by the chair,” they noted.

    They added that in determining whether the committee had a quorum to advance the nomination, “It would depend on how they view our committee rules from the 118th that we practice under for the 119th versus what the Senate rules are.” The staffer noted they have not yet spoken with committee Democrats or Democratic leadership about prepares for such an inquiry.

    Industry observers note that democrats also previously boycotted a committee markup in March over an aviation safety bill left off the committee’s agenda, after which action was deferred. The committee later came to agreement and rescheduled the markup.

    In their letter Monday, Democrats quoted Cruz from a 2014 statement about the nomination of Loretta Lynch to be attorney general.

    “As you wrote in 2014, controversial nominees ‘should not be confirmed in the lame duck session of Congress by senators who just lost their seats and are no longer accountable to the voters.’ We agree,” the letter stated.

    On Tuesday, Sen. Ben Ray Luján, D-N.M., wrote his own letter to Cruz calling for the removal of the nomination from the agenda based on grounds that Thumann Severs lied to the committee.

    It has been revealed that “While Ms. Thumann testified she did not work ‘on any media-related issues,’ documents obtained through Freedom of Information Act requests demonstrate that she worked on several media related issues, including on commitments that Skydance made to pave the way for FCC approval of its merger with Paramount,” Luján wrote.

    Democrats have criticized the FCC and Carr for allowing media consolidation, including by Skydance. There has also been bipartisan criticism of Carr’s threats against broadcasters for speech he disagrees with.

    Luján told reporters Wednesday prior to the markup that he expects, under Democratic control next year, Carr and potentially Thumann Severs would be called to testify.

    In a recent development, “I have questions. I certainly hope that Brendan Carr will voluntarily show up to this committee when invited, and that other rules and tools do not need to be used,” Luján remarked, responding to a question about possibly subpoenaing Carr. “But . . . everything should be on the table.”.

    According to recent reports, sen. Jerry Moran, R-Kan., remarked at the markup that he spoke with Thumann Severs about her role at the FCC and her “lack of engagement” as the commission has made decisions regarding broadcasters. He also said he found her testimony at last week’s nomination hearing “comforting.”.

    “I have concerns with FCC action in regard to political speech, broadcasters, and she indicated in her answers . . . in a way that provided me with a level of comfort about her nomination in regard to that glitch,” Moran noted.

    Moran also noted he hopes to meet with Thumann Severs before her nomination is brought to the floor.

    #226100. Latest Update: How to Spend Christmas in Paris

    📅 14 Dec 2017 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2367 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cntraveler ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: How to Spend Christmas in Paris

    📅 14 Dec 2017 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2367 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

    ⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Strasbourg may be France’s holiday capital, claiming the country’s oldest Marché de Noël, but there’s no denying Christmas in Paris is a showstopper.
    • In a recent development, oyster stands are as much a fixture of the holidays in Paris as Christmas markets—which happen to be one of the best places to try them.
    • Read our complete Paris travel guide here, which includes:.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Strasbourg may be France’s holiday capital, claiming the country’s oldest Marché de Noël, but there’s no denying Christmas in Paris is a showstopper. The city shines brighter each year with thousands of lights illuminating its famous squares and landmarks like the Champs-Elysées, dubbed the “world’s most beautiful avenue.” Holiday cheer seeps into each of the 20 arrondissements, decorated with larger-than-life garlands, forests of bauble-strewn fir trees, sculptural light displays, and wooden chalets doling out vin chaud (mulled wine) and holiday specialties like foie gras—best spread on subtly sweet pain d’épices (gingerbread).

    In a recent development, oyster stands are as much a fixture of the holidays in Paris as Christmas markets—which happen to be one of the best places to try them. Fête the season in true French fashion with a movable feast dining and drinking at some of the city’s most iconic institutions, from Left Bank cafés where famous writers and artists once gathered to the Palace hotels huddled around Place de la Concorde and Place Vendôme. And when you’re ready to indulge in Paris’s renowned retail therapy, swing by one of the grand magasins (department stores), which rank among the best in the world for their holiday window displays—Latest York City included—executed with the same style and precision as a couturier. The city may not be blanketed in snow, but the holiday spirit is as strong here as on the slopes in the French Alps—and even has the cuisine and chalets to prove it. If you’re planning to spend Christmas in Paris, you’ll find plenty of ways to celebrate, but these nine are some of the best things to do and see during the holidays in the City of Light.

    Read our complete Paris travel guide here, which includes:.

    Sources indicate that every review on this list has been written by a Condé Nast Traveler journalist who knows the destination and has visited that activity. When choosing things to do, our editors consider landmarks and experiences that offer an insider’s view of a destination, keeping authenticity, location, service, and sustainability credentials top of mind. This gallery has been updated with new information since its original publish date. Additional reporting by Lindsey Tramuta.

    Sources indicate that this winter, Oscar winner Cate Blanchett will lead the lighting ceremony of the 2 million LED lights illuminating the Champs-Elysées, running all the way up to the Arc de Triomphe. Sparkling each evening from 5:00 pm to 1:00 am, the most iconic avenue in Paris and its 400 balloon glass garland-adorned trees are coordinating with another famous landmark—the Eiffel Tower—twinkling in unison on the hour. Every quarter of an hour, the Champs-Elysées will put on a light show set to Vivaldi’s Four Seasons, and on December 24 and 25, the avenue will glow in Christmas-themed green and red. As part of the Newly introduced Year’s Eve countdown to midnight under the Arc de Triomphe, when a music-themed fireworks show will ring in 2027, the lights will shine in a tricolor blue, white and red display running down the avenue. Making a grand return after a decade-long pause, a Christmas market will run from the Place de la Concorde to the Arc de Triomphe with more than 200 stalls and an ice rink near the Pavillon Ledoyen.

    Dining with a view takes on a whole new meaning as you settle in by the panoramic windows on Ducasse sur Seine, the sole electric boat cruising the river. The floating restaurant is as gastronomic an experience as anything on land thanks to Alain Ducasse, the namesake chef behind the modern Parisian cuisine who claims a record-setting number of coveted Michelin stars. With chef Jean-Philippe Berens and the team prepping everything fresh on board, you’ll have prime views of the Seine while dining in style on Christmas Eve during the six-course menu, which features everything from silky foie gras royale to raw scallops topped with gelée and caviar—plus a cheese course with 18-month-matured truffled Comté.

    It has been revealed that the ambiance is equally as elegant at Ducasse Baccarat, where the chef’s cuisine is presented in an opulent space dripping in chandeliers and tableware designed by the French fine crystal creator. One of the few spots open daily during the holiday season, the restaurant ups the ante on Christmas Eve and Fresh Year’s Eve with themed degustation menus.

    France’s Capital of Christmas, Strasbourg, is home to the country’s oldest Marché de Noël, but Paris is dotted with more than a dozen markets and Christmas villages—the largest being La Magie de Noël in the Tuileries Garden, stretching from the Louvre to Place de la Concorde, which remains open until early January. There, you’ll discover hundreds of wooden cabins selling small gifts and seasonal treats; a selection of stands run by French artisans, from glassblowers to woodworkers; and attractions like a small ice rink and carnival rides—the Ferris wheel being the highlight, especially during the Eiffel Tower’s hourly light show.

    In a recent development, on the Square René Viviani, directly across from Notre Dame, you’ll find an intimate market with some 30 exhibitors selling regional food, hot chocolate, and handmade crafts. On the Left Bank, the Saint-Germain-des-Prés Marché de Noël unfolds along the namesake boulevard, next to the church, with wooden chalets and gourmet stands serving up everything from caviar and foie gras to Savoyard favorite tartiflette (a reblochon cheese and potato gratin) and sweet and savory pretzels. Unfolding in the courtyard of the Gare de l’Est train station, the historic starting point for the first Orient Express, the Marché de Noël des Producteurs Alsaciens is dedicated to Alsatian delicacies, with stands displaying regional specialties like kougelhopf, a fluted brioche cake filled with rum-soaked raisins and almonds.

    More than the decorated avenues and elaborate window displays, it is the Bûche de Noël (yule log cakes that may or may not be shaped like logs) that takes the lead as the ultimate holiday essential during Christmas in Paris. While most cakes are prepared and sold for take-away, there are a few spots to linger over tea and an individual slice of the indulgent Christmas cake, including Fouquet’s Paris, where the red, velvety chocolate and roasted corn mousse dessert is designed after the arabesques in the hotel’s historic salons and staircases. At Butterfly Pâtisserie, the Hôtel de Crillon’s boutique and tearoom, pastry chef Matthieu Carlin’s exquisite selection of seasonal pastries, including his Bolivian dark chocolate mousse Bûche de Noël, shaped like a submarine out of Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea—a tribute to the hotel’s Jules Verne-inspired holiday theme—can be enjoyed on-site with a cup of tea or a thick hot chocolate, or taken to-go. On the Place de la Concorde, snack on praline hazelnut and pistachio and orange blossom-flavored French toast from the hotel’s garland-strewn, striped winter chalet, or sip espresso martinis at Terrasse Concorde’s pop-up bar, which has been redecorated to mimic the most exclusive of ski resorts with French cashmere house Kujten’s custom-crafted cushions and blankets.

    Industry observers note that at Ritz Paris, craft your own yule log during a baking class, or settle in by the fireplace of the opulent, champagne-colored Salon Marie-Louise for a Christmas tea, where you’ll indulge in spruced-up takes on the afternoon tradition, including truffle cream finger sandwiches, lobster focaccia, and Crêpes Suzettes prepped à la minute. Next door, Ritz Paris Le Comptoir’s carousel-shaped Bûche de Noël has been deemed the city’s most stunning this season—and with only 65 available, it’s a gift unlike any other. Nearby at Mondovi Luxury Suites, chefs come to you for in-suite macaron-making sessions and mixology workshops—and with the “world’s best bartender” Colin Field behind the Le 7 Cocktail Bar, you’ll be learning from the best. On the Left Bank, the palace hotel Mandarin Oriental Lutetia Paris is serving a lavish Sunday brunch buffet, winter-themed afternoon tea with hot chocolate, and pastry chef Nicolas Guercio’s wreath-shaped yule log filled with layers of vanilla mousse, pear confit, and housemade pecan praline.

    Dating back to the mid-13th century, Sainte-Chapelle was once a royal chapel constructed to house the precious Crown of Thorns relic. Today, it’s admired for a different reason: the 15 stained-glass windows—comprised of 1,113 panels—are some of the most impressive in France, let alone all of Europe. Combine sightseeing with an experience only taking place during the holiday season listening to the music of Antonio Vivaldi or Johann Strauss during a classical concert within the chapel’s Gothic nave.

    It has been revealed that paris’s grand magasins (department stores) offer more than retail therapy. Their elaborate holiday window displays executed in couture-like fashion have earned them the title of best in the world—and that even includes Newly introduced York City. There’s a theme for every taste: The Samaritaine has been designed to feel like you’re taking a Christmas stroll through a snowy Paris, with winter lights and snowflakes crowning the grand magasin’s facade near the Seine. Shop at the indoor Christmas market and rest assured your presents will sit pretty under the tree this year thanks to the help of the pros at the dedicated wrapping studio, who can swath gifts in plush paper and custom-made ribbons. Over at Printemps Haussmann, behind the Opéra Garnier, the department store decorated its windows around the theme of “A Well-Knit Christmas," commissioning artisan-crafted crochet pieces; 160 animated characters (including felt cats and mice) chasing a ball of wool; and costumes by the store’s seamstress, Valérie Cuter.

    Sources indicate that at Galeries Lafayette Haussmann, holiday cheer doesn't end at the sidewalk, where French fashion designer Jean-Charles de Castelbajac themed the vibrant window displays around tales of angels and Matisse-inspired shapes. The Christmas tree and holiday displays beneath the store's Art Nouveau dome are an annual event, comparable to New York City’s Rockefeller Center tree lighting. Always vibrant and impressive, visitors who venture into the atrium of the shop this season will find a tree towering 16 meters high—but this year, the wing-shaped structure follows the animated storybook theme with an angel hovering overhead and a soundtrack by French DJ Vladimir Cauchemar. From the 30-foot-long Glasswalk footbridge, on the third floor of the store, you can catch an even better view of the “tree”—and snap a few photos. Hotels like SO/ Paris, on the banks of the Seine, are also dressing up for the occasion with paper artist Maud Vantours’ sculptural Nutcracker creation, which you can admire while sipping seasonal coffee or an espresso martini along with a slice of the hotel’s Bûche de Noël.

    In a recent development, nothing warms up locals and visitors like hot chocolate. For the most well-known, head to Angelina on the rue de Rivoli for its thick, decadent Chocolat Chaud Africain that will leave you wondering if they just melted an entire chocolate bar into your cup. If the line snakes around the block, take it à emporter. Near the Opéra Garnier, chocolatier Jade Genin (daughter of legendary Jacques Genin) is famous for her signature Concorde obelisk-shaped chocolate pyramidions, but her modernized take on hot chocolate—entirely plant-based with homemade almond milk—is as much a draw during the holidays. In Saint-Germain-des-Prés, Les Deux Magots’s scarlet banquettes may have been where the literary set like Jean-Paul Sartre once held court, but the cafe is also one of the best on the Left Bank for hot chocolate—where it’s prepared the traditional way, with melted Valrhona blended with warm milk and poured out of a classic carafe.

    While you can spike your hot chocolate with Irish whiskey and Chantilly cream, the city’s leading cocktail bars are taking some of the holiday season’s signature flavors and mixing them into creations like Beurre, Little Red Door’s cocktail version of fresh brioche, with crisp apple, butter, vodka, and yes—bread. At The Cambridge Public House, classic Irish coffee is given a French twist with calvados and silky salted maple cream, while Hôtel Lancaster partnered with historic French tea house Damman Frères for a gingerbread punch blended with rooibos de Noël tea and sherry, served alongside a tonka bean and gingerbread pastry.

    In a recent development, moulin Rouge’s lavish costumes adorned with sequins and rhinestones feel all the more festive when you’re dressed up yourself on Christmas night for a gourmet feast followed by the iconic Féerie revue show. At the Musée des Arts Forains (Fairground Museum), its annual Christmas extravaganza, Le Festival du Merveilleux, runs from December 26, 2026, to January 3, 2027. The makeshift Christmas village transforms into a light-strewn theater with magicians, aerial silk dancers, musicians, puppeteers, and tap dancers putting on dreamlike performances around the Belle Époque funfairs and gardens.

    It has been revealed that on Christmas Eve and Christmas Day, get your culture fix while sightseeing, sipping champagne, and listening to an orchestra perform carols and violin concertos during a classical Christmas show in one of the world’s most famous landmarks: the Eiffel Tower. And for the full winter wonderland experience, Disneyland Park’s characters are adorned in holiday attire during Christmas parades, musical performances by The Arendelle Carollers in the new World of Frozen, and meet-and-greet moments with Santa hat-clad favorites like Stitch.

    Recent findings suggest that embrace the festive feel of slope-side specialties like fondue at Chalet des Îles, a historic wooden Swiss chalet reconstructed by Napoleon III for Eugénie that hovers on an island in the Bois de Boulogne. Top Chef contestant and co-founder of Paris’s Ambos restaurant, Pierre Chomet, is behind this season’s fireside feast of Alsatian-style tartes, flambées, and creamy Mont d’Or cheese, while Park Hyatt Paris-Vendôme’s timber-clad Chalet du Park has popped up for the season in the Palace hotel’s terrace, serving winter menus designed by Michelin-starred chef Jean-François Rouquette.

    Sources indicate that at Hôtel Le Grand Mazarin, join a chocolate expert for small-group tastings, or take a seat for Christmas Eve dinner at candlelit restaurant Boubalé for a Mediterranean take on traditional plates like toasted challah with foie gras and fig and scallops wrapped in kadaif (shredded phyllo) paired with a holiday-themed DJ set. A dinner worth dressing up for, two Michelin-starred Le Clarence, off of the Champs-Elysées, has designed a feast worthy of royalty complete with the finest of ingredients, from dive-caught scallops to lobster and caviar—plus a collector-worthy wine pairing that fêtes the season in true French fashion.
