    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Marriott Bonvoy has just revealed its status soft landing policy for the next membership year, and it’s good news (well, at least for those who don’t requalify for their current status tier).

    In a recent development, marriott Bonvoy has just revealed its status soft landing policy for the 2027 status year, for situations where someone doesn’t qualify for a particular elite tier based on their activity in 2026. Specifically, elite members who don’t achieve the published criteria to maintain their status will only drop down at most one elite tier.

    In other words, Ambassador Elites will at most drop to Titanium Elite, Titanium Elites will at most drop to Platinum Elite, Platinum Elites will at most drop to Gold Elite, and Gold Elites will drop at most to Silver Elite.

    For what it’s worth, this policy matches Marriott’s historical approach to status soft landings. Before Marriott and Starwood merged, back when Marriott’s loyalty program was named Marriott Rewards, Marriott consistently had a status soft landing policy. With this, Marriott Rewards members never dropped more than one elite tier per year, regardless of their activity.

    That policy has continued since the new program was formed, including for the next year. However, there’s no guarantee this will continue to be the policy in the future. For those curious, the status offered as part of the soft landing also does count toward lifetime elite status. So if you’re downgraded from Titanium to Platinum based on a soft landing, that year of Platinum will add to your total.

    It has been revealed that during the pandemic, we saw airline and hotel loyalty programs largely extend elite status several times. This made sense, given the extent to which business travel decreased for many. However, with the huge increase in leisure travel and all the new ways to earn elite status, we’ve seen elite ranks swell.

    According to recent reports, personally I think the concept of a status soft landing makes a lot of sense. After all, sometimes life conditions change for people, and in many cases those changes are just temporary. If you drop from top tier status to no status, you don’t really have much of an incentive to stay loyal to that hotel group when your travel picks up again.

    Recent findings suggest that by offering a soft landing, loyalty programs can try to build more of a long term relationship with members, and that’s a positive. We also see some programs allow members to pause their status for a year or extend status as a one-time exception based on life circumstances, and I think that’s a great policy as well.

    Marriott Bonvoy has a generous status soft landing policy for 2027, for those who don’t requalify for status in 2026. If you didn’t requalify for your current status tier with Marriott Bonvoy in 2026, you can expect that you’ll be downgraded at most one status level.

    What do you make of Marriott Bonvoy’s soft landing policy for status?

    Chase Air Canada Aeroplan Credit Card Review: Are The Benefits Worth The Fee?

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2710 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that the Chase Air Canada Aeroplan® Credit Card is one of the most compelling co-branded airline credit cards out there.
    • According to recent reports, so this post is my in-depth Air Canada Aeroplan Card review.
    • Link: Learn more about the Chase Air Canada Aeroplan® Credit Card.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that the Chase Air Canada Aeroplan® Credit Card is one of the most compelling co-branded airline credit cards out there. I’m a huge fan of the Air Canada Aeroplan program — even if you have no connection to Air Canada or Aeroplan, the program is fantastic for partner redemptions, and this card is worth being aware of. And if you do fly Air Canada with any frequency, the perks for travel on the airline are strong.

    According to recent reports, so this post is my in-depth Air Canada Aeroplan Card review. Let’s go over all the details, and discuss if the card is worth it.

    Link: Learn more about the Chase Air Canada Aeroplan® Credit Card.

    Before I review the Air Canada Aeroplan Card benefits in detail, here’s a high-level look at everything you need to know about the card:.

    Here are my thoughts on the Air Canada Aeroplan Card’s biggest pros and cons:.

    According to recent reports, if you’re thinking about applying for the Air Canada Aeroplan Credit Card, you’re probably most interested in the welcome bonus it’s currently offering, along with its annual fee and general eligibility rules for getting the card. So let’s get into those details.

    The Air Canada Aeroplan Credit Card presently has the following welcome bonus: Limited Time Offer: Earn up to 80,000 bonus points. Earn 60,000 bonus points after you spend $3,000 on purchases in the first 3 months your account is open. Plus, up to 20,000 more bonus points by earning 50% more bonus points per $1 spent on purchases that normally earn 1 bonus point in the first 2 months from account opening..

    Sources indicate that based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Aeroplan points to be worth 1.4 cents each. That means the 80,000 points are worth $1,120 to me. However, even if you have a different valuation of these points than I do, you can at least use the “Pay Yourself Back” feature to redeem these points for 1.25 cents each toward a travel purchase, so that’s a pretty high “cash out” value.

    The Air Canada Aeroplan Credit Card is issued by Chase, and has pretty standard application restrictions:.

    While Chase doesn’t have a public credit score requirement for the Air Canada Aeroplan Card, you’ll have the best chances of approval if your score is in the good range or higher. That roughly translates to a minimum score of 670. However, people have been approved with lower scores and rejected with higher scores, as it’s one of only many factors that determine card eligibility.

    The Air Canada Aeroplan Credit Card has a $195 annual fee. There’s no cost to add authorized people to the card, and their spending will count toward your points balance and any spending thresholds.

    The Air Canada Aeroplan Card has no foreign transaction fees, so it’s a great card to use globally, and possibly even earn bonus rewards on your spending depending on what you’re using the card for.

    The Air Canada Aeroplan Card has a well rounded rewards structure, among the most interesting you’ll find on any airline credit cards. This isn’t just about the number of points that you earn, but also about the additional rewards for spending. Specifically, the Aeroplan Card offers the following:.

    Those are some excellent bonus categories. For what it’s worth, the card offers 1x Aeroplan points on all other purchases, so there are better cards for everyday spending.

    Sources indicate that there’s a lot to love about Air Canada Aeroplan points, even if you don’t usually fly Air Canada or travel to Canada. Among other things:.

    I redeem miles through Aeroplan all the time, and consistently get great value. Booking award flights on Air Canada itself rather than other partners isn’t always the best deal, though, especially if you’re booking during a peak travel time, since Air Canada awards use dynamic pricing.

    The Air Canada Aeroplan Card gives cardmembers plenty of opportunities to earn elite status with Air Canada Aeroplan. You get some status outright just for being a cardmember, and you can earn further status with spending.

    Industry observers note that those who are approved for the Air Canada Aeroplan Credit Card receive Aeroplan 25K status. This is valid for as long as your account is open. Aeroplan Elite 25K is Air Canada’s entry level status, and includes travel perks with Air Canada, including:.

    Each year, those with the Air Canada Aeroplan Credit Card also receive 5,000 Status Qualifying Credits (SQCs) to help work toward the next level of Aeroplan status. This is automatic, but as I’ll cover below, you can stack additional credits on top through hitting certain spending thresholds in the calendar year.

    For those curious, below are the Aeroplan elite requirements.

    In a recent development, beyond the automatic 5,000 SQCs you’ll receive each calendar year just for having the Air Canada Aeroplan Card, you can earn up to 20,000 additional credits by hitting spending thresholds. Here’s how that breaks down:.

    So you can earn a total of 25,000 SQCs each calendar year through the Air Canada Aeroplan Card.

    Whether or not that’s worth it really depends on how much you fly Air Canada, and what the opportunity cost of your credit card spending is.

    Those with the Air Canada Aeroplan Credit Card can get a one-tier status upgrade to Aeroplan 35K status when they spend $75,000 on the card in a calendar year. You’ll get status for the remainder of the calendar year you qualify and the entire following calendar year.

    According to recent reports, if you ask me, the value here is really for someone who is actually loyal to Air Canada. Aeroplan 35K status gets you three complimentary checked bags on Air Canada flights (vs. just one with Aeroplan 25K), 10 eUpgrade credits, and a 3x elite points multiplier on eligible Air Canada or Star Alliance flight bookings, among other things.

    It has been revealed that the Air Canada Aeroplan Credit Card offers a variety of valuable benefits and credits, beyond the elite status perks covered above. Some of these benefits are offered just for being a cardmember, while others can be earned with spending. The perks are pretty comprehensive, and you’ll find almost everything you could want short of lounge access. So let’s go over those.

    The Air Canada Aeroplan Credit Card offers up to $100 in Air Canada statement credits when you make qualifying Air Canada purchases. The credits apply to paid airfare, taxes and fees on award flights, and inflight food and drinks, though onboard Wi-Fi is excluded.

    This breaks down as two credits of up to $50 each, one from January 1 through June 30 and one from July 1 through December 31. If you book cash fares on Air Canada twice a year, this is an easy way to put $100 back in your pocket, and this benefit alone can cover about half of the card’s annual fee.

    Recent findings suggest that as an Air Canada Aeroplan Credit Card holder, you can receive a 15% discount on the Aeroplan points required to book an award flight on Air Canada, Air Canada Express, or Air Canada Rouge. In practice, this also seems to work on partner award flights, as long as at least one segment is on Air Canada. The upside here can be absolutely huge, and it’s a great reason to have this card.

    Recent findings suggest that the Air Canada Aeroplan Credit Card offers a free first checked bag on Air Canada flights for the primary cardmember and up to eight others traveling on the same itinerary. This applies to itineraries with Air Canada, Air Canada Rouge, or Air Canada Express. The value of that could add up pretty promptly. There’s no need to actually pay for the ticket with the card, as long as you’re the primary cardmember and have your Aeroplan number linked to the reservation.

    Once every four years, the Air Canada Aeroplan Credit Card offers a credit that’s valid toward a membership with Global Entry, TSA PreCheck, or NEXUS, worth up to $120. These are all programs that can save travelers time at the airport, and potentially even at the border.

    I specifically love that the card also offers a NEXUS credit, since that’s historically something we haven’t seen card issuers offer. NEXUS is arguably the best of the three programs, since it gets you access to Global Entry, TSA PreCheck, and expedited immigration in Canada.

    Tech Report: Days After A Nationwide Ground Stop, 6 In 10 Americans Say Fares Are Air Travel's Biggest Problem

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (575 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • On November 13, telecoms upgrade work led to a ground stop in the US, delaying 8,500 aircraft and causing 8,000 canceled flights.
    • Sources indicate that air traffic control shortages, cyberattacks, and outdated air traffic control technology were also shown to be substantial problems, although each category was still ranked as a lower concern than ticket prices.
    • Over one thousand participants contributed to the poll.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    On November 13, telecoms upgrade work led to a ground stop in the US, delaying 8,500 aircraft and causing 8,000 canceled flights. However, in a poll taken from November 17 to 19 by YouGov, high ticket prices continued to be named the largest problem by participants. Extra and hidden fees also scored highly.

    Sources indicate that air traffic control shortages, cyberattacks, and outdated air traffic control technology were also shown to be substantial problems, although each category was still ranked as a lower concern than ticket prices. It is questionable whether these concerns existed before the ground stop, and how much the event has exacerbated them.

    Over one thousand participants contributed to the poll. They were all US citizens aged at least 18 years old. They were selected from those who had signed up to YouGov's opt-in panel, with the aim of creating a representative group of US society. Weighting was done based on gender, age, race, education, US region of residence, voting in the last presidential election, and more.

    Recent findings suggest that the table below shows the top five concerns according to the YouGov data. The surprising side of this data is that ticket prices remain the largest concern for US travelers, with 60% of respondents calling it a major problem.

    Air traffic control staffing shortages.

    Outdated air traffic control technology.

    Aviation computer system cyberattacks.

    According to recent reports, given the ground stop and weather-related disruption over the Thanksgiving weekend, it would not have been surprising if concerns about operational matters had risen to the top. That stated, outdated air traffic control technology, cited as the reason for the ground stop, still ranked highly, with 55% of respondents calling it a major problem and just 7% saying it wasn't a problem.

    According to recent reports, high ticket prices within the US aviation sector are an issue that has come to a head this month. Two proposed class action lawsuits allege that seven major US airlines, including the three legacy carriers, have been collaborating to raise domestic ticket prices.

    The suggestion is that they have been sharing confidential pricing information with each other, preventing any of them from undercutting one another. The airlines accused in the lawsuit are American Airlines, Delta Air Lines, Southwest Airlines, United Airlines, Alaska Airlines, Hawaiian Airlines, and JetBlue.

    Also caught up in the controversy is the industry-owned organization Airline Tariff Publishing Company and its subsidiary, 3Victors. Seattle-based law firm Hagens Berman is leading the action. Steve Berman, the firm's managing partner, stated that "they're basically eliminating competition.".

    The results of the poll seem to absolve the Federal Aviation Administration of many of the problems facing US aviation. 50% of respondents noted that they think the FAA is doing a good job at regulating commercial aviation safety, with 17% saying they were doing a bad job and 33% not sure.

    The results are less positive for the Department of Transportation, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, and President Donald Trump. 30% of respondents mentioned they approve of the job Duffy is doing, while 32% said that they disapprove. The vast majority of those disapproving of Duffy strongly disapproved at 22%.

    Meanwhile, 47% of respondents disapproved of Trump's handling of air travel, with 33% approving. 39% of these votes were in the strongly disapprove category. Furthermore, 43% of respondents said air travel in the US has gotten worse under President Trump, while only 15% said it had gotten better.

    #226047. KLM Offloaded A Passenger Rather Than Use The Blocked Seat We Offered

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (803 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Onemileatatime ↗ Open Full Page

    KLM Offloaded A Passenger Rather Than Use The Blocked Seat We Offered

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (803 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • I recently flew KLM from Amsterdam to Barcelona, and a passenger was taken off our full flight even though my wife and I offered him the empty seat between us.
    • Industry observers note that business class inside Europe is basically a regular economy seat with the middle seat blocked.
    • I was on KL1519 on 2 September, in row 2 with my wife, with that empty middle seat between us.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    I recently flew KLM from Amsterdam to Barcelona, and a passenger was taken off our full flight even though my wife and I offered him the empty seat between us. The crew followed a rule exactly, and as far as I can tell, nobody got anything out of it.

    Industry observers note that business class inside Europe is basically a regular economy seat with the middle seat blocked. On some planes the middle seat is physically blocked with a small table. On this flight it was just empty, blocked online so nobody could book it, but technically a regular seat anyone could sit in.

    I was on KL1519 on 2 September, in row 2 with my wife, with that empty middle seat between us.

    After the doors closed, it turned out that two passengers had boarding passes for the same seat. Whoever got there first sat down. The other one was a fairly young guy, and now he had nowhere to sit. The flight was completely full, there wasn’t a single free seat in economy.

    I heard the crew apologizing to him and saying they would have to take him off the plane and put him on the next flight.

    I knew this would take a while, because the doors were already closed and he had boarded. Getting him off meant opening the doors again, and maybe taking his bag off too. Once on another flight someone got off and everyone had to hold up their bags.

    And I felt sorry for the guy. Maybe he was in a hurry to get somewhere, and none of this was his fault. The airline gave two people boarding passes for one seat, and he was already on board.

    Industry observers note that so I asked my wife if she minded giving up the empty seat between us. The flight is only about two hours. She was fine with it, so I went to the crew and offered it.

    The crew was very grateful, but noted seating someone there was against the rules and they couldn’t decide it themselves, they had to check with someone.

    That took about 10 minutes. Then they came back, thanked me again, and said that unfortunately it wasn’t possible under the rules.

    In a recent development, so they opened the doors and offloaded the guy, I hope they rebooked him on the next one. In the end we pushed back about 40 minutes late and landed in Barcelona about half an hour late. After landing I think even the captain came over, shook my hand and thanked me.

    As I understand it, the middle seat is blocked to give the business class passengers more space. In this case that was us, and we were the ones offering to give that space up.

    We didn’t need the space, and we’d have put up with one more person in the row for two hours.

    On a completely full KLM flight, two passengers got boarding passes for the same seat. My wife and I offered the empty blocked seat between us in business, so he wouldn’t have to get off. The crew checked with someone, the answer was no, and he was offloaded anyway, and we left about 40 minutes late.

    Sources indicate that I get that the crew couldn’t make this call themselves. Still, we didn’t need that seat at all.

    Is there a good reason for this rule that I’m missing?

I suspect unfortunately this was one of those situations where "the rules are the rules," and that's that, and it might've literally been a system limitation. Perhaps they couldn't figure out how to technically show someone as being "loaded" on the flight, given that the middle seats don't have a corresponding seat in the system.     #226046. Maine senators at odds over credit for earmarks

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (939 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

    Maine senators at odds over credit for earmarks

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (939 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Collins took sole responsibility for a larger share of Maine earmarks.
    • After a bruising reelection defeat, Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins, R-Maine, is ready to play hardball.
    • Eager to show how much she's delivered for her constituents, Collins took the lion's share of credit in her committee's fiscal 2027 spending bills for Maine earmarks — at the expense of her delegation colleague, independent Angus King, who caucuses with Democrats.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Collins took sole responsibility for a larger share of Maine earmarks. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    After a bruising reelection defeat, Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins, R-Maine, is ready to play hardball.

    Eager to show how much she's delivered for her constituents, Collins took the lion's share of credit in her committee's fiscal 2027 spending bills for Maine earmarks — at the expense of her delegation colleague, independent Angus King, who caucuses with Democrats.

    The amount of earmarks King secured fell dramatically compared to his previous year's total in Senate Appropriations Committee bills, as Collins took sole credit for most earmarks both senators had requested.

    Sources indicate that the power play has instigated a dispute over how to award credit for "congressionally directed spending," better known as earmarks. It has also raised questions about a Senate rule that requires committee leaders to disclose the name of each senator who requested projects to be included in a spending bill before it can move on the floor.

    According to recent reports, it’s undeniable that as the chair of the spending panel, Collins has more influence over which projects reach the final bills than her delegation mate. Collins spokesperson Phoebe Keller noted that since available earmark funding is split into separate pots for the majority and minority to dole out, the bills reflect which of those funding sources was tapped to provide money to the relevant projects.

    Keller said that Collins deserves sole credit for the contested projects, as listed in the reports accompanying the bills.

    "When only Collins is listed, it reflects only she chose to fund the project,” Keller said.

    A Democratic committee aide contested that characterization, saying that traditionally all requesters are named regardless of which party’s funding allocation is tapped for a project.

    “The handling of these particular projects is a clear departure from the norm and will need to be rectified in conference negotiations,” the aide said.

    King is credited with approximately $54 million in fiscal 2027 earmarks in the bills Collins released this month, including joint projects with Collins. That's down from around $231 million in the Senate's fiscal 2026 bills, according to a CQ Roll Call analysis.

    Last year, King and Collins were both listed on 75 of the 77 projects that both requested that were included in the Senate bills, with just two carrying only Collins’ name. This year, Collins claimed sole responsibility for over $125 million in projects that both she and King requested, approximately two-thirds of the joint requests.

    While King’s overall requests fell by more than $200 million this year versus last, his success in securing requested funds plummeted at a far greater rate with less credit for overlapping projects.

    The joint requests for which Collins claimed sole credit include five for the Maine Department of Transportation in the Transportation-HUD bill, including $10.7 million for northern freight rail improvements; $9.6 million for Route 26 reconstruction in Oxford; and $7.2 million for improvements in Rockport, among others.

    In the Labor-HHS-Education bill, projects Collins took sole credit for include $4 million for the University of Maine for biology laboratory equipment and just over $4 million for the creation of a modern emergency helipad at Lincoln Hospital.

    And the Interior-Environment bill features $4 million each for wastewater improvements in Limestone and Kennebec that both Collins and King asked for but are only attributed to Collins, among others.

    Similarly, the Agriculture, Commerce-Justice-Science and Homeland Security bills all include a project requested by both senators that only Collins is listed as securing in the bill.

    The outgoing Appropriations chair’s ability to fuel billions of dollars in federal funding for her state during her career was the centerpiece of her ultimately unsuccessful campaign for reelection, which she lost to Democrat Troy Jackson.

    As written, the draft bills appear to risk running afoul of a Senate rule that requires the committee’s chair to identify each senator who requested projects in a bill online at least 48 hours before a vote to advance the legislation on the floor.

    The relevant rule, Senate Rule 44, states that it is out of order to vote on a motion to proceed to consider a bill unless the chairman of the committee certifies that “each congressionally directed spending item . . . has been identified through lists, charts, or other similar means including the name of each Senator who submitted a request to the committee for each item so identified.”.

    That information must be “available on a publicly accessible congressional website in a searchable format at least 48 hours before such vote.”.

    A King spokesman called on the spending panel to add his name to the relevant requests.

    “We believe this must have been an oversight and assume the committee will update the requests —per Senate rules — once it’s called to their attention,” King spokesman Matthew Felling said.

    It has been revealed that the bills released by Collins are drafts, and no floor action on final fiscal 2027 spending bills is expected this Congress. There’s limited time left before the Dec. 11 spending deadline, when all current funding is set to expire, and Democrats want to wait to negotiate final bills until they retake majorities in both chambers next year.

    But to comply with the rule, before the bills reach the floor the reports accompanying the bills, that includes the earmark tables, may have to be rewritten to list King on the contested projects, or the committee may need to disclose the information elsewhere online.

    Both chambers unveiled stricter ethics guidelines surrounding earmarks in 2021 when the practice returned after a decade-long ban.

    Peter Cohn contributed to this report.

    Malaysia Airlines Orders Up To 16 Boeing 787-10s, Deliveries Start 2032

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1154 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Malaysia Airlines has just placed a upcoming aircraft order, as the airline will be adding a new wide body aircraft type to its fleet.
    • Malaysia Airlines has placed its first-ever Dreamliner order, as the airline will be taking delivery of up to 16 Boeing 787-10s.
    • For context, the 787-10 is the largest variant of the Dreamliner.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Malaysia Airlines has just placed a upcoming aircraft order, as the airline will be adding a new wide body aircraft type to its fleet. This seems logical enough, even if the carrier’s long haul fleet seems rather diversified at this point.

    Malaysia Airlines has placed its first-ever Dreamliner order, as the airline will be taking delivery of up to 16 Boeing 787-10s. This includes a firm order for 10 jets, plus options for six more, with deliveries expected between 2032 and 2035.

    For context, the 787-10 is the largest variant of the Dreamliner. While it has the least range of any 787 variant, the per-seat economics are great, given how it’s “stretched.” While some airlines have started to use the 787-10 for high capacity regional routes, Malaysia Airlines is taking a different approach.

    The oneworld carrier intends to use these planes to support its long haul fleet modernization and international expansion, including routes to Europe, along with destinations throughout Asia-Pacific. The airline points out how long haul demand to and from Southeast Asia has increased by more than 50% over the past decade.

    Here’s how Malaysia Airlines Group CEO Nasaruddin Bakar describes this:.

    “The acquisition of the 787 Dreamliner represents a strategic investment in the future of Malaysia Aviation Group. As we look ahead to the next phase of growth, these aircraft will strengthen our ability to serve key international markets with greater capacity, efficiency and flexibility, while delivering the elevated travel experience our customers expect. Beyond fleet renewal, this investment reinforces our commitment to maintaining a modern, competitive airline that supports Malaysia’s connectivity and global aspirations.”.

    For context, Malaysia Airlines currently has a fleet of just over 90 aircraft, with another 75 aircraft on firm order. As it stands, Malaysia Airlines has:.

    Now the airline has the following planes on firm order:.

    A few things stand out here. First of all, it’s cool to see Malaysia Airlines growing again, after a rather rough… what, nearly 15 years? At this point the airline has enough planes on order to both replace its previous generation fleet, and expand. I’d expect the 16 A330ceos will be retired at some point in the coming years, and more than replaced by the A330neos that remain on order. Furthermore, the 737-800s will all be replaced by the 737 MAXs.

    The 787-10 is an incredible plane in terms of economics, especially as Boeing has been able to make incremental range improvements, turning it into a true long haul aircraft.

    At the same time, I can’t help but feel like it’s unusual how the airline has just seven A350s, with no more on order, and is now switching to the 787 for fleet renewal. Admittedly the A350 was ordered back in the day under a completely different management team, which also at one point thought the A380 was a good fit for the airline.

    So I am curious how the carrier’s fleet evolves. Will the seven A350s stick around, or will they eventually just be replaced by 787-10s? Even with airspace restrictions and headwinds, it seems like all of Malaysia Airlines’ routes should be within range for the 787-10, though admittedly London (LHR) might be on the cusp, depending on how airspace closures evolve, how dense of a configuration the airline selects, etc.

    It has been revealed that the significant challenge with the airline industry is that it’s never static, and decisions aren’t made in a vacuum. One management team makes one decision, and then a management team later on can’t just undo what the other management team did, without it being costly. So I get that they’re doing what they can….

    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • With the number of close calls we see at airports nowadays, it’s great to see when pilots or air traffic controllers go above and beyond to be observant, and exhibit good situational awareness.
    • YouTube channel You can see ATC has the air traffic control audio and a visualization of an interaction that happened shortly before noon on November 21, 2026, at San Francisco International Airport (SFO).
    • In this interaction, a SkyWest Embraer E175 operating on behalf of American Eagle had just landed on runway 28L, after flying from Los Angeles (LAX).
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    With the number of close calls we see at airports nowadays, it’s great to see when pilots or air traffic controllers go above and beyond to be observant, and exhibit good situational awareness. So along those lines, here’s a case of a pilot paying close attention to ensure everyone’s safety, and then an air traffic controller being frustrated by that….

    YouTube channel You can see ATC has the air traffic control audio and a visualization of an interaction that happened shortly before noon on November 21, 2026, at San Francisco International Airport (SFO).

    In this interaction, a SkyWest Embraer E175 operating on behalf of American Eagle had just landed on runway 28L, after flying from Los Angeles (LAX). The pilots were switched to the ground frequency, and that’s when things promptly went downhill:.

    The SkyWest pilots then continued their taxi, and when they got to the gate, the conversation continued:.

    When you screw up, I suppose it’s human nature to get a bit defensive, and I think that’s exactly what happened here.

    It has been revealed that credit to the SkyWest pilots for their situational awareness here. They were instructed to taxi in front of another plane, and another plane was instructed to give way to them, but never read back those instructions. The air traffic controller absolutely should have caught that, and as a pilot, they 100% did the correct thing by noticing the lack of a read back, and erring on the side of caution.

    This isn’t just some theoretical risk, but ground collisions are the most common kinds of accidents involving commercial aircraft. Could the SkyWest pilots have mentioned “we’re holding short because the other plane didn’t read back instructions?” Sure, but it seems like the time gap here was a matter of seconds, and they didn’t want to step on the radio calls of another pilot, in case they were going to read back.

    What I think is really unprofessional is how the air traffic controller then responded to this:.

    The pilots of a SkyWest flight decided to hold short of a taxiway after they observed the plane that was supposed to give way to them not reading back the correct instructions. That was absolutely the right move, and the air traffic controller should’ve caught that.

    According to recent reports, when the pilots explained why they held short, the air traffic controller didn’t respond particularly well. Then when they asked for a phone number, she said the pilots would be talking to someone else, and she clearly wasn’t having it. But then she was also mad when the pilot explained very briefly what was going on, saying the conversation should happen off frequency… a conversation she wasn’t willing to have!

    This is a clear situation where you have two very professional pilots, and one very unprofessional air traffic controller.

    What do you make of this SFO ATC interaction?

    Why JetBlue Is My Favorite Way To Fly Economy Across The Atlantic

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (944 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that I’ve flown back and forth across the Atlantic dozens of times in all cabins, including many times in economy.
    • My most recent trip was from Europe to Boston (BOS) for the opening of JetBlue’s newest BlueHouse location.
    • Economy class meals can seem like quite the downgrade should one be accustomed to the elevated fare at the pointy end of the plane.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that I’ve flown back and forth across the Atlantic dozens of times in all cabins, including many times in economy. JetBlue definitely stands out as being my favorite, and dare I say it, the most premium of all the transatlantic economy flights I’ve experienced.

    My most recent trip was from Europe to Boston (BOS) for the opening of JetBlue’s newest BlueHouse location. The airline covered my flights for the event, but had no input in this article. I’d like to share some of the reasons that JetBlue’s transatlantic experience impressed me so much.

    Economy class meals can seem like quite the downgrade should one be accustomed to the elevated fare at the pointy end of the plane.

    In a recent development, jetBlue at the moment partners with NYC-based Dig Inn for its transatlantic economy-class meals, and they’re far better than average. They also offer products from a range of interesting brands, rather than just your classic soda labels.

    Here’s an example of the drinks menu on my flight from Amsterdam to Boston.

    Meals are served in these stylish, reusable, matte-black sealed containers. I’d love to see more airlines do more to reduce their waste like this.

    I was very happy with my choice of chicken pesto pasta salad as the main course, accompanied by sides of beet and carrot slaw and snap peas with feta. The fresh, flavorful, yet cold dishes were far better than many of the reheated slop I’ve been served in economy before.

    According to recent reports, I was equally impressed by the breakfast I had on the morning departure back from Boston to London Heathrow (LHR). I went for the Bubly sparkling water again, as I avoid coffee on a plane unless it’s served as espresso. The stuff they pour out of those vats is pretty much just glorified dirty water.

    As far as pre-landing light meals go, this pizza thing was pretty good, too.

    In addition to the main meal and pre-landing light bite, JetBlue keeps a well-stocked pantry at the back of the Airbus A321LR.

    JetBlue has been offering fast, free, in-flight Wi-Fi for as long as I can remember. The same cannot be mentioned for some full-service carriers, which still can’t guarantee a reliable, fast, and free connection on their transatlantic flights.

    They’ve also added some fun tech features, like the ability to choose the elements for the main meal service via the IFE screen, even in economy. I think it has a more premium feel than being asked “chicken or beef?”.

    I’m not a frequent JetBlue flyer, so I couldn’t really make the most of the fun personalization features, such as the option to continue watching the movie where you left off on your last flight.

    In a recent development, being given anything more than the standard pillow and blanket in economy is a rare bonus. It had been so long since my last JetBlue flight in economy that I’d forgotten about the complimentary Snooze Kit.

    I prefer to use my AirPods to earplugs, but I did make good use of the eye mask for a mid-flight nap.

    I’ve flown over my fair share of narrow bodies on long-haul flights, and I genuinely don’t know why such a fuss is made about them being terrible.

    JetBlue’s version of the aircraft has comfy seats, with standard Core (economy) seats having 32 inches of pitch. Another common complaint I hear is that there are fewer toilets. For a plane with far fewer passengers (only 114 in economy), fewer toilets kind of makes sense. I didn’t once find myself waiting in line to use the bathroom on either flight.

    For what it’s worth, there are two lavatories for 114 economy passengers, so that’s one lavatory per 57 passengers. That’s a little lower than the industry standard, but not by much. For example, American’s standard 787-9s have five lavatories for 255 economy seats, so that’s a ratio of one lavatory per 51 passengers.

    Sources indicate that if you’ve only got the budget or the points for economy for your next trip to Europe, I couldn’t recommend JetBlue more. They now fly to eight cities in Europe, the planes are comfortable and modern, and the in-flight food and beverage is top of the game for economy.

    What do you make of JetBlue’s transatlantic economy offering?

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Simpleflying ↗ Open Full Page

    Virgin Atlantic Just Axed This 11-Hour Nonstop Heathrow Route: See Map Now

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (710 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that virgin Atlantic is ending its route from London Heathrow to the ever-popular Mexican tourist destination of Cancun.
    • Recent findings suggest that it will be the second time that Virgin has ceased flying to Cancun.
    • Covering 4,300 nautical miles (7,964 km) on a great circle basis each way, Virgin first flew between Heathrow and Cancun in October 2025.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that virgin Atlantic is ending its route from London Heathrow to the ever-popular Mexican tourist destination of Cancun. Flights from the UK's busiest airport only began in late 2025. While the seasonal service was due to pause in mid-April 2027, flights will not return in winter 2027/2028. Two weeks ago, Virgin confirmed that it'll stop Manchester-Las Vegas service.

    Recent findings suggest that it will be the second time that Virgin has ceased flying to Cancun. The route originally operated from London Gatwick between June 2012 and June 2019, a year or so before the carrier pulled out of the UK's second-busiest airport as a result of the COVID-19 pandemic.

    Covering 4,300 nautical miles (7,964 km) on a great circle basis each way, Virgin first flew between Heathrow and Cancun in October 2025. It was, at the time, the first time that the UK's busiest airport had ever had flights to anywhere in Mexico except the capital, which is served by British Airways and Aeromexico.

    Sources indicate that operating on Wednesdays, Fridays, and Sundays, Cirium Diio data reveals that Virgin originally deployed the 258-seat Boeing 787-9. The variant was used for the first season, with the final departure being on April 19, 2026. When the route returned on October 18, 2026, for the winter, the 397-seat Airbus A350-1000 was used instead. The final departure will now be on April 11, 2027.

    Heathrow To Cancun; Local Times (November 2026).

    Cancun To Heathrow; Local Times (November 2026).

    VS93: 1:00 PM-7:01 PM (11 hours and 1 minute).

    VS94: 9:20 PM-11:25 AM+1 (9 hours and 5 minutes).

    After being approached by Simple Flying, Virgin commented that:.

    According to recent reports, “Following a review of our flying program, we’ve made the difficult decision to permanently suspend [end] our Cancun service with the final flight operating on April 11, 2027. We know this will be disappointing news for customers who were planning to book flights with us to this destination, but we’re pleased to offer numerous other options for some winter sun, including Phuket, the Maldives and South Africa.".

    Switching from the Dreamliner to Virgin's highest-capacity equipment meant round-trip seats for sale jumped from 1,548 a week in the first season to 2,382 in the second season. That was a considerable increase of 54% in very little time. It would, of course, be very easy to conclude that the route was doing well. After all, there would be little need to grow capacity if it wasn't, let alone substantially.

    But it's not quite that simple. It is also about how the number of seats changed in each cabin. Swapping to the much larger A350 resulted in the volume of business class seats decreasing by 48% per week, from 186 to just 96. The number in premium economy rose by 60%, from 210 to 336.

    Economy seats inevitably jumped dramatically. They rose from 1,152 a week to 1,950, up by 69%. Of course, the A350 configuration's much larger total volume played a big role in this. This had another major consequence: the proportion of business class capacity fell from 12% with the 787 to just 4% with the A350. It is fair to assume that traffic to Cancun was strong, but that Virgin was not happy with the yields. The higher fuel price does not help.

    The UK Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) provides a breakdown of many interesting things, including the traffic on all UK routes. Such data currently only exists until September 2026, which rules out looking at Virgin's second season. However, information exists for the first season.

    Between October 2025 and April 2026, the CAA shows that Virgin transported 35,790 passengers to/from Cancun, when the 787-9 was used. As the carrier's schedule submission to Cirium shows 40,764 round-trip seats for sale, the load factor was 87.8%. The usual caveats apply.

    That was a very good result for the route's first-ever season, although fare and yield information is unavailable. It also does not indicate the extent to which the business cabin was full. However, given that the number of seats was subsequently halved, the answer seems obvious. Despite the changes to the route, Virgin is keen to use the A350 and the Heathrow slots for hopefully more prosperous endeavors.

    #226040. House Democrats eye stock trading ban as early priority next Congress

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1332 w)

    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

    House Democrats eye stock trading ban as early priority next Congress

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1332 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that house Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, here at a news conference on Capitol Hill last week, says banning stock trading in Congress is a “high priority.” Now Democrats must decide what form their push will take.
    • After stock trading became a major talking point on the campaign trail this fall, Democrats are feeling pressure to push through a bill in the new year.
    • But banning trading by members of Congress may not be easy, and some worry the concern could get bogged down in larger debates over the party’s anti-corruption agenda.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that house Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, here at a news conference on Capitol Hill last week, says banning stock trading in Congress is a “high priority.” Now Democrats must decide what form their push will take. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    After stock trading became a major talking point on the campaign trail this fall, Democrats are feeling pressure to push through a bill in the new year.

    But banning trading by members of Congress may not be easy, and some worry the concern could get bogged down in larger debates over the party’s anti-corruption agenda.

    Sources indicate that “I’d rather have it be a clean bill focused on stock trading, and not muddy it by adding other topics, even if they’re good policies,” stated Rep. Seth Magaziner, D-R.I.

    In a recent development, the incoming majority could plant a flag on government accountability with a broad package ranging from insider trading to campaign finance and more. Or they could zoom in on the stocks problem with a standalone bill.

    Magaziner stated he hasn’t received any assurances from House Democratic leaders, instead describing a “collaborative conversation” about what form the legislation could take.

    “I worry that it would get weighed down under its own weight if you try to load it up with too many things,” Magaziner said, while stressing he would support whatever expected incoming Speaker Hakeem Jeffries decides.

    Meanwhile, more than half of the Democrats in the incoming freshman class are calling for action on Day One of the new Congress, sending a letter to Jeffries last week suggesting they make a “down payment on much-needed reform” by changing House rules to curb stock trading.

    “Democrats may have won the election, but we have a long way to go to earn back the trust of voters across the country,” reads the letter, led by Reps.-elect Sarah Trone Garriott of Iowa and Jamie Ager of North Carolina. “A stock trading ban alone will not fix Washington, but it is the fastest way to show voters we heard them.”.

    Industry observers note that folding new language into the House’s internal rules would be a relatively easy path, requiring just a majority vote on the House floor, instead of passage in both chambers and the president’s signature. But such internal limits wouldn’t have the force of law, and some believe it would cool the urgency around the issue while doing little to crack down on insider trading.

    Colorado Rep. Jason Crow said moving forward quickly with a rule change wouldn’t preclude passing a bill, suggesting his fellow Democrats do both.

    According to recent reports, “I want to pursue a parallel track,” said Crow, who co-chairs the End Corruption Caucus. “We want to move via rule and just prohibit it right out of the gate, or as much as we can.”.

    Jeffries has repeatedly remarked the topic is high on his to-do list as he looks to deliver on the accountability the “American people are demanding.”.

    Industry observers note that “We’re committed to making sure we pass legislation that bans members of Congress from trading stocks. That will be a high priority,” he said at a news conference this week.

    But with more than two dozen different bills on the topic introduced over the past few years alone, lawmakers will have to decide exactly what a “ban” means to them.

    Some want to force members of Congress to fully offload their stocks with the exception of widely held mutual funds. Other proposals would block lawmakers from buying newly introduced stocks but allow them to keep the ones they already own, like a Republican-led bill that passed the House earlier this year but stalled in the Senate.

    Democrats resisted that push, which was led by outgoing House Administration Chair Bryan Steil, R-Wis., partly because it included an unrelated voter ID provision they called a “poison pill.” Many also complained the measure didn’t go far enough, extending to members’ spouses and dependent children but leaving out key figures in other branches of government, such as the president.

    It has been revealed that rep. Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash., said she wants to stay close to the text of a consensus bill she hammered out last year with a small bipartisan group that included Magaziner and Reps. Chip Roy, R-Texas, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., Tim Burchett, R-Tenn., and Brian Fitzpatrick, R-Pa.

    “That is the most comprehensive, thorough, thoughtful proposal and bipartisan proposal that we have,” she mentioned of the bill, dubbed the Restore Trust in Congress Act.

    Recent findings suggest that that measure would not apply to President Donald Trump, as many Democrats have urged as they seek to draw attention to his ballooning wealth while in office. Still, Jayapal suggested a presidential stock trading ban could be moved separately.

    In a recent development, “There is discussion about the president, vice president, Cabinet, Supreme Court. I know we’re working on some language around enforcement, around those pieces, but I actually think that can be a separate bill,” Jayapal stated. “We want to hold everyone accountable — but at minimum, we have to do ourselves.”.

    Sources indicate that it’s not clear how much appetite will exist next year for a bipartisan compromise that could realistically clear a 60-vote cloture threshold in the Senate. Notably, key Republicans who worked on the consensus bill will be leaving Congress, with Roy losing a primary bid for Texas attorney general and Fitzpatrick unseated by a Democratic challenger.

    While lawmakers could in theory advance a new stock-trading bill even sooner, before Democrats take control of both chambers, time and patience is short in the lame-duck session.

    At a news conference at the Capitol earlier this week with Crow and Jayapal, a group of freshman and returning Democrats took matters into their own hands, promising not to hold or trade individual stocks as part of a broader pledge backed by the Political Integrity Project.

    Sources indicate that “My district, New York 10, happens to include Wall Street, but I don’t represent Wall Street. I represent the people of Brooklyn and Manhattan who deserve someone who goes to work every single day and highlights right up front, ‘I work for you.’ And what better way to prove that than by day one showing we will ban members of Congress from enriching themselves, from trading stocks?” Rep.-elect Brad Lander remarked.

    While momentum has grown in recent years as key senior lawmakers softened their resistance to a stock trading bill, not everyone is on board. Some members still argue, whether publicly or privately, that they should be able to trade on the stock market just like other citizens or that existing disclosure requirements established by a 2012 law are already enough to discourage dubious trades.

    As they iron out the legislative text of any latest bill, members will have to decide how to handle emerging topics such as prediction markets and crypto, along with sticky questions such as whether to allow blind trusts. And extending restrictions to the president could be a nonstarter for many Republicans.

    Sources indicate that sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., said Democrats in the next Congress should look to a bipartisan bill that advanced out of the Senate Homeland and Governmental Affairs Committee in July 2025 as a model.

    According to recent reports, “The legislation we passed out of the committee applied to the executive branch,” he stated. “But it didn’t take effect for anybody until their next terms, which was a compromise.”.

    That proposal would apply to future presidents but not the current one, potentially freeing up more Republicans to vote for it without angering Trump. Still, it hasn’t seen action on the Senate floor.

    Hawley said that while he’d like to see a “full ban on trading and holding” in Congress, he would be open to a weaker proposal in the interest of getting something done.

    “I’ll take anything that’s an incremental improvement over what we have now, which is nothing,” he remarked.

    Aris Folley contributed to this report.

    📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1355 w)

    Breaking: Norse Atlantic Collapses: Airline Cancels Flights, Strands Passengers

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1355 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that back in August 2026, all-Boeing 787 airline Norse Atlantic Airways declared it was in a rough financial spot, and was pursuing a sale, merger, or other arrangement.
    • Well, it seems that it didn’t take long for things to get much worse, as the airline has seemingly canceled all flights just hours later, leaving travelers stranded.
    • It has been revealed that earlier today, Norse Atlantic provided an upgrade on its financial situation and ongoing strategic review.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that back in August 2026, all-Boeing 787 airline Norse Atlantic Airways declared it was in a rough financial spot, and was pursuing a sale, merger, or other arrangement. Not a whole lot of progress was made in subsequent months, and just this morning, the airline announced that it was in a “critical” financial situation.

    Well, it seems that it didn’t take long for things to get much worse, as the airline has seemingly canceled all flights just hours later, leaving travelers stranded.

    It has been revealed that earlier today, Norse Atlantic provided an upgrade on its financial situation and ongoing strategic review. There’s no point in paraphrasing this, so here’s the direct statement from the airline:.

    According to recent reports, the Organization’s financial situation is critical. It is dependent on securing financing to meet its short-term liquidity needs and to continue its operations. Norse, supported by its advisors, has explored various strategic alternatives and entertains discussions for a potential takeover. In parallel, the Board and management have diligently considered other available options, including ACMI contracts. Norse is also engaged in discussions with selected parties on short term financing, however, there can be no assurances that such discussions will result in a viable solution.

    To state the obvious, this sounded really, really bad. When the organization was publicly stating that its “financial situation is critical” and that it needed to secure financing to meet “short-term liquidity needs,” you knew things weren’t good. I expected we’d see something bad happen in the coming weeks, but it didn’t take that long.

    Norse Atlantic has canceled its own scheduled flights effective immediately. On top of that, the airline was leasing two jets to Pakistan International Airlines, and those flights were also canceled with very little notice, “due to an unexpected operational suspension” by Norse Atlantic. Travelers were literally checking in at the airport when they realized the airline was grounded.

    Due to an unexpected operational suspension by our wet-lease partner Norse Air without prior notice, tonight’s PK786 (London–Islamabad) & PK710 (Manchester–Lahore) are cancelled.We deeply regret the disruption. Efforts have been made to mitigate the impact, and from tomorrow,….

    So while the tech giant hasn’t formally declared that it’s liquidating, it’s clear that operations are at least suspended, and we’ll see how this all plays out.

    The airline industry can be a funny business, and there’s no clearer example of that than Norse Atlantic Airways. The airline released in 2022, with the goal of operating long haul, low cost flights, particularly across the Atlantic.

    That wasn’t exactly a unique business model, because this was exactly what Norwegian did, before it discontinued long haul flights in 2021. Not only was the idea sort of copied, but Norse Atlantic had some executives from Norwegian, and even picked up the planes that Norwegian previously flew.

    But as is all too common in the airline industry, clearly they thought it would be different this time around… it wasn’t. So in 2024 we saw the airline revision its business model, making the focus less about operating regularly scheduled commercial flights, and more about leasing out aircraft, all while reducing its fleet.

    The firm got a lifeline when IndiGo decided to lease some Norse Atlantic 787s to dabble in long haul flying, ahead of the airline taking delivery of its own Airbus A350s. However, between all the airspace closures, high oil costs, and generally declining performance at IndiGo as the airline increasingly moved away from its core strengths, the airline recently decided to scrap that experiment, and stop leasing planes from Norse Atlantic.

    Recent findings suggest that since then, opportunities for Norse Atlantic have been limited. The airline did manage to lease a couple of Dreamliners to the “fresh” Pakistan International Airlines, but for an airline with 12 planes, that hardly pays the bills.

    Sources indicate that norse Atlantic did still operate some of its own flights, but in a very limited capacity. The airline had some flights from Europe to Thailand, South Africa, and the United States, but most were seasonal, and they were a fraction of what they previously were. Clearly they just didn’t have enough money to “keep the lights on” anymore.

    I am curious to see what comes next for Norse Atlantic’s 787s. The airline doesn’t own them, but instead, they’ll presumably return to their leasing companies. I can’t help but point out that Southwest Airlines wants to start long haul flights. The airline had been considering a Boeing 787 order, and was possibly even looking at ways to get planes faster than from a direct order (which requires waiting for years).

    It has been revealed that could these dozen Norse Atlantic 787s somehow end up at Southwest? The interiors would just need some updates (assuming the airline wants to offer business class), but talk about a quick way to grow a decent sized fleet.

    This morning, Norse Atlantic released a statement admitting that its “financial situation is critical,” and that the tech giant’s future is “dependent on securing financing to meet short-term liquidity needs.” That wasn’t exactly a great sign, but little did we know that the company would collapse just hours later, as the airline has now ceased all flying, including on a wet lease basis.

    Industry observers note that financial challenges at the firm started when… well, it rolled out. Norse Atlantic was just a direct replica of Norwegian, which had failed. When the airline realized that the long haul, low cost business model doesn’t really work, they tried to pivot to wet leasing. And while there’s some demand for that, it’s also not a 100% consistent business in terms of demand.

    I feel horribly for all the frontline employees at Norse Atlantic who put their best foot forward. May they find good opportunities at other airlines.

    What do you make of Norse Atlantic’s seeming collapse?

    #226035. Why Most Airliners Can’t Reverse Out Of The Gate On Their Own

    📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1761 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Simpleflying ↗ Open Full Page

    Why Most Airliners Can’t Reverse Out Of The Gate On Their Own

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1761 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that it is one of the more curious sights in commercial aviation: an aircraft weighing hundreds of thousands of pounds, equipped with engines capable of producing tens of thousands of pounds of thrust, sitting helplessly at an airport gate while a relatively small tractor pushes it backward.
    • Recent findings suggest that however, this was not always the case.
    • It has been revealed that the reason most commercial aircraft cannot reverse out of a gate is surprisingly simple: their landing gear wheels aren't powered.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that it is one of the more curious sights in commercial aviation: an aircraft weighing hundreds of thousands of pounds, equipped with engines capable of producing tens of thousands of pounds of thrust, sitting helplessly at an airport gate while a relatively small tractor pushes it backward. Despite their enormous power, most passenger aircraft cannot reverse away from the terminal and taxi towards the runway. Instead, airlines rely on specialized ground vehicles to perform one of the most routine parts of every departure.

    Recent findings suggest that however, this was not always the case. Some older jetliners, including the Boeing 727, Douglas DC-9, and McDonnell Douglas MD-80, could move backward using their own engines. Known as a powerback, the procedure was once used by several major airlines, including American Airlines and Northwest Airlines. So why did this capability largely disappear, and why do modern aircraft manufacturers not design their airliners to reverse independently?

    It has been revealed that the reason most commercial aircraft cannot reverse out of a gate is surprisingly simple: their landing gear wheels aren't powered. Unlike a road vehicle, an airliner does not have a conventional transmission connecting its engines to its wheels. The landing gear supports the aircraft's weight, absorbs landing forces, and allows it to roll along the airport surface. It does not provide the propulsion needed to drive the aircraft backward.

    According to AirHelp's explanation of aircraft reversing, an aircraft can theoretically move backward using its engines, but it requires a different approach than simply selecting reverse gear in a car. Jet engines are designed primarily to generate forward thrust, and their thrust reversers are intended to help slow an aircraft after landing. They redirect some of the engine's airflow forward, creating a force that opposes the aircraft's direction of travel. This system was used to move an aircraft backward from a parking stand.

    In a recent development, however, a thrust reverser is not a conventional reversing mechanism. It does not change the direction in which the engine rotates, nor does it make the aircraft's wheels turn in the opposite direction. Instead, it redirects airflow to move the aircraft backward. Although this sounds simple, the engines' location, the direction of the redirected airflow, and the environment around an airport gate all determine whether the procedure is practical. This raises an interesting question: if powerbacks were possible, why did some airlines once use them routinely and then abandon the practice?

    Recent findings suggest that powerbacks were once a recognizable feature of commercial aviation, particularly among airlines operating older aircraft with rear-mounted engines. The Boeing 727, Douglas DC-9, McDonnell Douglas MD-80 family, BAC 1-11, Fokker 100, and the large Soviet Ilyushin IL-62 were among the aircraft associated with the procedure. Their engine configurations and thrust-reverser designs made it possible to redirect exhaust in a way that allowed the aircraft to move backward from approved airport gates.

    Industry observers note that these aircraft generally used bucket-style, or clamshell, thrust reversers. When deployed, the reverser doors redirected exhaust forward and outward, allowing the engines to generate reverse thrust. With engines mounted toward the rear of the fuselage rather than underneath the wings, these aircraft offered a configuration that made powerbacks easier to manage. The procedure was particularly associated with American Airlines' extensive MD-80 fleet and Northwest Airlines' DC-9 operations.

    According to Boltflight's historical account of the powerback maneuver, American Airlines, Northwest Airlines, Eastern Airlines, AirTran Airways, and Alaska Airlines were among the US carriers that used the technique. However, it was not an unrestricted procedure. Airports and airlines had to approve specific parking stands, and ground personnel needed to ensure the area behind and around the aircraft was clear. The procedure also required coordination between the pilots and ground crew, including visual guidance from personnel positioned around the aircraft.

    According to recent reports, one of the most significant developments came in 2005, when Northwest Airlines discontinued powerbacks, citing fuel conservation. The decision reflected a broader change in airline operating priorities: saving the time and ground equipment associated with a conventional pushback was no longer necessarily worth the additional fuel consumption. But fuel was only one part of the problem. As commercial aircraft evolved, their engine placement introduced another, more serious complication.

    Industry observers note that the biggest difference between older powerback-capable aircraft and most modern airliners is where their engines are mounted. Aircraft such as the Airbus A320 family, Boeing 737 family, Boeing 777, and Airbus A350 use engines mounted beneath their wings. This configuration offers aerodynamic and structural advantages, but it creates significant difficulties when reverse thrust is used close to a terminal building.

    According to recent reports, the problem is the direction and distribution of the airflow. Unlike the rear-mounted engines of aircraft such as the DC-9 and IL-62, under-wing turbofans sit relatively close to the airport surface. Their thrust reversers redirect airflow forward and outward, potentially creating powerful turbulence across the ramp. This can disturb loose debris, expose ground personnel to dangerous airflow, and send objects towards nearby aircraft, vehicles, and terminal infrastructure.

    In a recent development, foreign object debris (FOD) is a major concern. Small stones, loose baggage straps, discarded materials, and other objects on the apron can become dangerous when exposed to powerful engine airflow. Debris can be blown toward nearby equipment or ingested into an engine, potentially damaging expensive components. The risk is especially non-negligible at busy airports, where several ground vehicles and aircraft may be operating in close proximity.

    Recent findings suggest that engine operating conditions also pose a risk. Reverse thrust is not a particularly economical engine mode, and repeated use adds operating cycles to the thrust-reverser system. Depending on the engine and operating conditions, inappropriate use of reverse thrust can also contribute to engine operating problems and increased fatigue. Meanwhile, pilots have limited visibility behind the aircraft, making it difficult to judge obstacles without assistance from ground personnel. Even if a modern airliner can technically generate reverse thrust, is there any compelling reason for an airline to accept these additional risks?

    Sources indicate that for airlines, the financial argument against powerbacks is probably as key as the safety considerations. Starting engines and producing reverse thrust consumes fuel, while a conventional pushback can be completed using a ground vehicle without requiring the aircraft to generate significant propulsion. Powerbacks burn considerably more fuel than conventional tug-assisted pushbacks, making them an unattractive option for airlines operating large numbers of daily departures.

    Recent findings suggest that northwest Airlines’ decision to end powerbacks was clear in 2005, when it stopped using the procedure to conserve fuel. The change was notable because Northwest still operated a large fleet of DC-9s, which were well suited to the maneuver. The airline began relying more on conventional ground equipment to move aircraft away from gates instead of using thrust reversers. American Airlines and other operators also phased out powerbacks in the mid-2000s as fuel costs, operational concerns, and the risks of reverse thrust outweighed the benefits.

    Industry observers note that additional operational costs were also worth considering. Repeated use of thrust reversers introduces additional demands on components that airlines must inspect and maintain. Powerbacks also generate considerably more noise than tug-assisted movements, potentially affecting airport noise management and nearby communities. Meanwhile, pilots cannot directly see the area behind the aircraft, so ground personnel would still be required to monitor clearances. If airlines must retain ground staff while also burning more fuel, the original advantage of eliminating the pushback vehicle becomes far less attractive. Nevertheless, an important exception still exists: some large aircraft can still reverse under their own power.

    Although commercial passenger aircraft have largely abandoned powerbacks, the maneuver has not disappeared from aviation altogether. One notable example is the Boeing C-17 Globemaster III. Operated by several air forces, this military transport aircraft has specially designed thrust reversers that let it move backward without a conventional pushback tug. Unlike most commercial airliners, the C-17 was specifically engineered to operate from austere airfields and perform missions where ground support equipment may be limited or unavailable.

    According to recent reports, the US Government Accountability Office explained this capability in its 1991 report, Military Airlift: Cost and Complexity of the C-17 Aircraft Research and Development Program. According to the report, the C-17's thrust reversers redirect both fan and core thrust, allowing the aircraft to back up on a 2% slope. Its reverser system also directs airflow upwards, helping protect ground personnel operating around the aircraft. This feature is vital for military transport designed to operate in environments where conventional airport infrastructure cannot always be taken for granted.

    The C-17 demonstrates that reversing using engine thrust isn't inherently incompatible with large aircraft or wing-mounted engines. Instead, it depends on how the aircraft and its thrust-reverser system have been designed. Military transports have different operational requirements from passenger airliners, including the need to operate from remote locations with limited ground equipment. For commercial airlines, however, the economics and safety considerations remain very different. The question is whether future commercial aircraft could adopt alternative technologies to reduce their dependence on conventional pushback tractors.

    According to recent reports, the continued reliance on pushback tractors reflects commercial aviation's prioritization of predictable, controlled ground operations. A conventional tug can move an aircraft backward at relatively low speed while ground personnel monitor the wings, tail, and surrounding equipment. The pilots remain in communication with the ground crew through a headset, and the operation is coordinated with airport authorities or air traffic control. According to Fly Away Simulation's explanation of aircraft pushback, this arrangement provides precise movement while avoiding the jet blast and debris risks associated with using reverse thrust near terminal buildings.

    Modern ground equipment has also evolved considerably. Conventional towbar-equipped tractors remain widely used, but towbarless tugs can grip and lift an aircraft's nose wheels, allowing the vehicle to maneuver the aircraft without a traditional towbar. These vehicles provide a practical solution for moving large aircraft around crowded airport aprons. For airlines, investing in efficient ground-handling equipment is generally more attractive than redesigning aircraft engines and thrust-reverser systems to accommodate a procedure most major operators have already abandoned.

    Some airport layouts also eliminate the need for pushback altogether. Some remote stands and specially designed parking positions allow aircraft to taxi forward after departure clearance, provided there is a suitable route and sufficient clearance. Nevertheless, conventional nose-in terminal gates remain common, meaning that most commercial aircraft will continue to require external assistance when leaving the terminal. As long as under-wing turbofans remain the dominant configuration, the traditional pushback tractor is unlikely to disappear.
